```text
---
scope: stryker.config.mjs, stryker.vitest.config.ts
verified-at: b70fe3924a
---

# mutation testing — StrykerJS for the frontend, go-mutesting for Go

**Read when:** running a mutation tool on changed files, writing a personal config, or a run that
stops before mutating anything.
**Not here:** how each test tier runs -> `testing.md`; the course deliverable and its file names ->
`COURSE-WORKFLOW.md`.

## Responsibilities

| Side | Tool | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `web_src/js` (Vitest) | StrykerJS with its Vitest runner | `package.json` devDependencies, `stryker.config.mjs` |
| Go packages | go-mutesting | `go install`, nothing in `go.mod` |

Gremlins is not used: its README warns that very big Go modules can take hours, and Gitea is one
module (`go.mod`).

## Key files

| Path | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `stryker.config.mjs` | Shared Stryker options: the Vitest plugin, ignore patterns read from `.gitignore`, runner, reporters. Names no files |
| `stryker.vitest.config.ts` | `vitest.config.ts` merged with `isolate: true`, used only by Stryker |
| `vitest.config.ts` | The normal Vitest config, with `isolate: false` |
| `.gitignore` | `/.stryker-tmp` (Stryker's sandbox), `/reports/mutation` (its reports), `/report.json` (go-mutesting's) |

## Conventions & invariants

- `stryker.config.mjs` sets no `mutate`. Personal configs import it, spread it, and change only
  report paths or similar; the files to mutate are passed on the command line with `--mutate`.
- Stryker copies the project into `.stryker-tmp/` before running. `stryker.config.mjs` feeds every
  `.gitignore` line to `ignorePatterns`, which Stryker matches with `.gitignore` semantics (`!`
  included), so the copy holds only what git tracks. `node_modules` is symlinked, not copied.
- `plugins` names `@stryker-mutator/vitest-runner` directly. Stryker's default `@stryker-mutator/*`
  search looks beside its own package, which pnpm keeps under `node_modules/.pnpm` without the
  runner, so the `vitest` option is then reported as unknown.
- The Vitest runner's `related` mode (on by default) runs only test files that import the mutated
  files, and `coverageAnalysis: 'perTest'` reruns only the tests covering each mutant.
- Stryker runs all related test files in one worker. With `vitest.config.ts`'s `isolate: false`,
  module state (such as a listener registered at import) leaks from one file into the next, so
  `stryker.vitest.config.ts` turns isolation on. Normal runs and CI keep `vitest.config.ts`.
- go-mutesting's built-in test step replaces the real source file with each mutant, runs that
  package's tests, and restores it. Only the package's own `_test.go` tests run, not `tests/`.
- go-mutesting always writes `report.json` to the directory it runs in; the `json_output` setting
  in its YAML config is not read. In its output, `PASS` means the mutant was killed.

## Recipes

**Run Stryker on some files.** From the repository root:
`pnpm exec stryker run <config> --mutate web_src/js/a.ts,web_src/js/b.ts`. The summary table is
printed at the end; `mutation.json` and `mutation.html` land in `reports/mutation/` unless the
config moves them. A run on one ~250-line module with ~40 related tests takes about a minute.

**Write a personal Stryker config.** A `.mjs` file that imports the shared one:

```js
import base from '<relative path>/stryker.config.mjs';
export default {...base, jsonReporter: {fileName: 'reports/mutation/<name>/mutation.json'}};
```

Paths inside it resolve from the directory Stryker runs in, so run it from the repository root.

**Run go-mutesting.**

1. Install: `go install github.com/avito-tech/go-mutesting/cmd/go-mutesting@master`. Its module
   path has no `/v2`, so its v2 tags cannot be installed by version, and building it needs the Go
   version its own `go.mod` asks for.
2. Run on files, with the Go version from `go.mod` so the tests match CI:
   `GOTOOLCHAIN=go<version> go-mutesting <file.go>... > <out>.txt`. The last line holds the score.
3. Check `git status`: no source file may be left changed. Move `report.json` where it belongs.

## Gotchas

- Stryker's "There were failed tests in the initial test run" means a related test fails on
  unchanged code. Rerun it with `pnpm exec vitest related <file> --run --no-file-parallelism` to see
  whether it only fails when files share a worker (an order-dependent test) or fails anyway.
- A Stryker `EISDIR ... copyfile` error comes from copying a symlinked directory; any such folder
  needs to be in `.gitignore` or `ignorePatterns`.
- Mutants that hit Stryker's timeout count as killed, and whether one times out can change between
  runs, so two runs of the same code can differ by a mutant or two.
- An interrupted go-mutesting run can leave a mutated source file behind. `git diff` shows it;
  `git restore <file>` undoes it.
- Each go-mutesting mutant recompiles and reruns the whole package's tests, so packages with
  database fixtures (`models/...`) are slow: time one `go test ./<pkg>/` first and multiply.
- Behaviour covered only by `tests/integration` shows up as surviving go-mutesting mutants.
- `make lint-js` lints the root `*.ts` files, not `.mjs` ones, and nothing under `docs/`
  (`Makefile`, `ESLINT_FILES`).

## Related

- `testing.md` — the test tiers the mutation tools run
- `build-and-tooling.md` — the lint and build targets
```

	dir := filepath.Dir(fileAbs)

	var conf = loader.Config{
		ParserMode: parser.AllErrors | parser.ParseComments,
	}

	if buildPkg.ImportPath != "." {
		conf.Import(buildPkg.ImportPath)
	} else {
		// This is most definitely the case for files inside a "testdata" package
		conf.CreateFromFilenames(dir, fileAbs)
	}

	conf.AllowErrors = true
	prog, err := conf.Load()
	if err != nil {
		return nil, nil, nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("Could not load package of file %q: %v", file, err)
	}

	pkgInfo := prog.InitialPackages()[0]

	var src *ast.File
	for _, f := range pkgInfo.Files {
		if prog.Fset.Position(f.Pos()).Filename == fileAbs {
			src = f

			break
		}
	}

	if src != nil {
		for _, c := range collectors {
			c.Collect(src, prog.Fset, fileAbs)
		}
	}

	return src, prog.Fset, pkgInfo.Pkg, &pkgInfo.Info, nil
}

The 125-character limit means I can't quote the whole D6 section in one block. Below are the key passages as short verbatim quotes, with paraphrase connecting them.

**What D6 is and which work it covers**

- D6 is a new individual deliverable. A mutation tool changes your code in small ways and checks whether your tests catch each change. Surviving mutants point to weak or missing tests.
- It applies to "**one of your issues whose PR changes source code and tests**." CSCI 535 students must do **two** such issues.
- Run the tool on "the **source files changed by your PR(s)**" for that issue, not the whole project.
- Analyze each surviving mutant as equivalent or as a test gap. If there are more than 10 survivors, analyze at least 10, "starting with those in lines your PR added or changed."
- Add or strengthen at least one test that kills a surviving mutant that revealed a gap, then re-run the tool to confirm.
- "A tool is required. Manual mutation does not count."

**Tool choice (quoted and paraphrased)**

- The doc's table maps stacks to tools: StrykerJS with the Vitest runner for Vitest projects, StrykerJS with the Jest runner for Jest projects, and Gremlins or go-mutesting for Go (Gitea backend).
- Each student configures and runs the tool on their own files and commits the configuration used.
- "You may reuse a teammate's setup (and are encouraged to)," as long as you "run the tool yourself and credit the teammate in your report."

**Evidence and submission**

- Commit before and after reports as `docs/sprint3/mutation/reports/<issue#>-<username>-before.json` and `-after.json` (`.txt` for go-mutesting).
- The write-up goes in `docs/sprint3/mutation/<issue#>-<username>.md`.
- Reported mutation scores must match the reports, and the mutant your new test kills must appear as killed in the "after" report.

**Write-up template**

- Header: "# Mutation testing: Issue #<N> -- <issue title>", followed by the PR(s), Tool, Config (with a teammate credit if reused), Command, Reports links, and Mutation score (before → after).
- Surviving mutants table with the header: "| Location (file:line) | Mutation | Equivalent or test gap? | Why |".
- New or strengthened test section: commit link, test name, and "Kills: [mutant location]".
- Questions:
  1. "What did the surviving mutants reveal about your tests?"
  2. Did any surviving mutant point to an assertion whose expected value was not based on the requirements?
  3. If you used AI to configure the tool, analyze survivors, or write tests, what did it produce and what did you verify or correct? If not, write "N/A."

**Zero or few surviving mutants**

- If no survivor reveals a gap, the doc says to state that and justify it in the surviving-mutants table. This completes the step.
- The 10-mutant threshold governs how many survivors you must analyze. The doc gives no further guidance for runs with very few mutants.

**Grading (D6 rubric, 15 points)**

- Tool run on the PR's changed files, with configuration, command, results, and reports committed: 4 points.
- Surviving mutants analyzed correctly, with an explanation: 4 points.
- At least one new or strengthened test kills a survivor, confirmed by a re-run: 4 points.
- Answers show understanding, not just description: 3 points.
- For CSCI 535, "the D6 score is the average of the two submissions."

**Blocked students**

- Ask teammates first, then the TA "as early as possible," with the errors and the AI log of what you tried.
- If the tool still won't work, "the TA may approve running the tool on a different issue" or a different part of your code.
- "Problems reported at the end of the sprint will not excuse a missing D6."

#144 Show which dependencies block a pull request from merging, and whether each is open, merged or closed
assignees: ab-wm
milestone: Sprint 3
state: OPEN

> Blocked by #143, which decides which dependencies block a merge.

## User Story

As a maintainer about to merge a pull request, I want its page to tell me which dependencies still block it, and whether each one is open, merged or closed, so that I know why it cannot be merged before I press Merge, not after.

## User Scenario
Sam's pull request #12 depends on pull request #11, which was closed without merging, and on issue #9, which is still open. When a maintainer opens #12, the merge box, where blockers such as missing approvals already appear, says "This pull request is blocked by its dependencies:" followed by links to #11 and #9, each with its repository and title. No merge button is offered.

In the sidebar, the "Depends on" list shows each entry's state: #11 "Closed", #9 "Open". Today both just look closed or open, and a merged pull request looks the same as a closed one. Once #9 is closed and #11 is reopened and merged, the merge box shows the merge button again.

| Dependency | Sidebar shows | Blocks merging (#143) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open issue or pull request | Open | Yes |
| Closed issue | Closed | No |
| Merged pull request | Merged | No |
| Pull request closed without merging | Closed | Yes |

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given a pull request with a dependency that blocks merging, when it is opened, then its merge box shows "This pull request is blocked by its dependencies:" followed by a link to each blocking dependency, shown as in the timeline: `owner/repo#N - title`.
- [ ] AC2: Given the same, when a user with merge rights opens it, then no merge button is offered, including its "(When checks succeed)" form; "Manually merged" stays offered where the repository allows it, as #143 leaves it unblocked.
- [ ] AC3: Given a pull request with no dependencies, or whose dependencies are all resolved, when it is opened, then the merge box looks as it does today.
- [ ] AC4: Given a blocking dependency the viewer cannot read, when they open the pull request, then the merge box counts it as "You do not have permission to read 1 dependency" without its title, as the sidebar does today.
- [ ] AC5: Given the "Depends on" or "Blocks" list in the sidebar of an issue or pull request, when it is shown, then each entry shows its state: "Open", "Closed", or "Merged" for a merged pull request.
- [ ] AC6: Given a repository with "Enable Dependencies For Issues and Pull Requests" turned off, when a pull request is opened, then neither the merge box nor the sidebar shows dependencies, as the sidebar does today.

## Out of Scope
- Which dependencies block a merge, and refusing the merge: Issue (#143)
- Showing dependencies on the issue and pull request lists.
- Changing how dependencies are added or removed.

## Open Questions
None

## Design Decisions
Added per commit during implementation, as in #53 and #54.

## Scope
medium (3 points). Touches two parts of the pull request page, the merge box and the sidebar's dependency lists, plus one new message; moderate changes to the page's data and templates, with browser tests for both parts.

## AI Disclosure
Used claude-code for the drafting of this issue, followed by my changes and proofing. Changes after the spec review were also made with claude-code.
```

**What a run on #143 would actually find**
- **Plenty of mutants, but few from this PR.** A run limited to the changed functions makes 203 mutants. Almost all of them are in code #143 didn't touch: the other checks in `CheckPullMergeable`, and the rest of the two merge handlers.
- **Only a handful on the lines #143 changed.** That's the dependency block in `check.go` and the one new error branch in each handler. I deleted the dry-run files, so I don't have an exact number.
- **The core rule produces nothing.** `MergeBlockedByDependencies` gets 0 mutants.
- **The handler mutants would survive, but for a tool reason.** Those handlers are only tested by `tests/integration`, which go-mutesting doesn't run. So D6 on #143 is still possible: you'd classify those survivors as unit-level gaps, then kill one by adding a handler unit test. But that test would exist mainly to satisfy the tool, because the integration tests already check the same branch.

**What the sprint page says**
- **Which issue:** D6 is "one of your issues whose PR changes source code and tests". Picking #144 is your choice. The TA only has to approve a different issue when the tool itself is blocked.
- **No-gap case:** if no survivor reveals a gap, you state that and justify it in the table. But one rubric line (4 of 15 points) is "at least one new or strengthened test kills a survivor, confirmed by a re-run". The page doesn't say whether the justification alone earns those points, so a run with no gaps puts them at risk.
- **Survivors to analyse:** you analyse at least 10, "starting with those in lines your PR added or changed". On #143 most of the 10 would be from code it didn't change.

**Why #144 fits better**
- **It has the kind of code the tool can mutate.** Its Go code decides which dependencies block a merge, labels each one Open, Closed or Merged, and counts the ones the viewer can't read (AC4). That's branching logic, and its unit tests would run in the same package.
- **The risks:**
  - The code doesn't exist yet, so the mutant count is unknown.

  - #144's code shouldn't be shaped around the tool; it should be written normally and mutated afterwards.

- (a) #144.
- (b) #143, with a handler unit test as the strengthened test.

I recommend (a). Its changed lines are the ones the tool can mutate, so the survivors you analyse would be from your own code.

Closes #59

## What changed and why

On GitHub, `c` starts a new issue or pull request from the list, and opens the commit picker on a pull request's changed files. Gitea had no such shortcut. Building on #56's registry and #58's link shortcuts, this PR adds `c` in those three places.

- **The create buttons declare `c` themselves.** "New Issue" and "New Pull Request" are links, so they declare `c` the same way #58's tabs declare their `g` shortcuts, and `c` goes where the button leads, exactly as a click would. When the repository uses issue templates, that is the template chooser.
- **Only a button that really creates something declares it.** An archived repository has no create button, and its pull request list shows "Compare commits" in that place; a "New Pull Request" button the user can't use is greyed out. The list page already decides all of this, so in each of these cases `c` simply doesn't exist.
- **The commit picker declares `c` itself.** It is a Vue component that builds its own button, so it adds `c` when it appears on the "Files changed" tab. `c` opens it as a click does, ending with focus on its first entry. It first moves focus to the picker's button, so Escape and the arrow keys work even while the commits are still loading, and it never closes an open picker.
- **Typing into a filter menu no longer runs a shortcut.** Gitea's older dropdowns without a search box jump to the item starting with a typed letter, but didn't mark the key as used, so `c` in the issue list's "Type" filter left for the new issue page instead of picking "Created by you". Gitea's patch for those dropdowns now marks the letter as used, which #56's registry already respects. This helps every shortcut, not only `c`. Only a letter typed on the dropdown itself is marked: typing into a filter box inside a dropdown's menu, such as the Label filter, works as before.
- **Each `c` is listed with what it opens** ("New Issue", "New Pull Request" or "Filter by commit"), under "Issues" on the lists and "Pull Requests" on the "Files changed" tab, using existing strings, so nothing new needs translating.
- The docs in `.claude-students` describe how a component adds its own shortcut.
- Like `s`, `t` and the `g` keys, `c` can't be turned off yet; #60 adds that setting.

## How the changes relate to the ACs

- **AC1:** `c` on the issue list goes where "New Issue" leads: the new issue page, or the template chooser.
- **AC2:** `c` on the pull request list goes where "New Pull Request" leads.
- **AC3:** a greyed-out "New Pull Request" button, and an archived repository's lists, declare no `c`, so it does nothing.
- **AC4:** on the "Files changed" tab, `c` opens the commit picker with focus on its first entry, and the arrow keys and Escape work as after a click.
- **AC5:** `c` only exists on those three pages, so it does nothing elsewhere; when `c` is the second key of `g c`, only `g c` runs.
- **AC6:** each `c` is described by what it opens, under "Issues" on the lists and "Pull Requests" on the "Files changed" tab.

## How it was tested

### Test strategy

Almost all of this PR is wiring: which button declares `c` is decided by the list page, and the commit picker only exists on a real pull request. So the tests are Playwright tests on real pages.

- **Unit tests for what a page can't show.** Which shortcuts the picker lists isn't visible anywhere until #57's dialog exists, so `web_src/js/components/DiffCommitSelector.test.ts` mounts the picker and checks that it lists `c` as "Filter by commit" in "Pull Requests" (AC6). Whether a dropdown marks a typed letter as used is invisible on a page too, so three tests in `web_src/js/modules/fomantic/dropdown.test.ts` check it directly: a letter typed on a dropdown without a search box is used and Ctrl+C isn't, while typing into a search box, a search box inside the menu, or an input in a menu item is left alone. Everything else is covered by earlier unit tests: #58's for a link turning into a shortcut, and #56's for `c` inside `g c`. Opening the picker is left to Playwright, because a unit test would have to fake the loading of the commits and the focus handling, and would mostly test the fakes.
- **Playwright tests for the wiring.** Each of the 6 new tests in `tests/e2e/shortcut.test.ts` sets up the situation where a mistake would show. A signed-in user who can write to the repository, because "New Pull Request" is only usable with write access or a fork; the same repository with an issue template, where "New Issue" leads to the chooser instead. Focus in the "Type" filter, where `c` is also the menu's own letter for "Created by you", and typing into the Label filter, whose search box sits inside its menu and must still take every letter. A signed-out visitor, for whom "New Pull Request" is greyed out, and an archived repository, where "Compare commits" takes its place and shares its `issue-list-new` class. A real pull request's "Files changed" tab, the only place the picker exists and the only way to see where focus lands, once normally and once with its commits held back, since focus only matters while they load.
- **What "nothing happens" means here.** For AC3 the tests check that the page declares no `c`, instead of pressing `c` and waiting to see that nothing happened. Showing that a key didn't start a navigation races with whatever is pressed next, and whether `c` exists is decided by the declaration alone.

**Testing the tests.** Each test was checked via mutation testing to ensure that the tests actually detect something real: declaring `c` on the greyed-out "New Pull Request" button, declaring it on "Compare commits" in an archived repository, removing it from "New Issue", letting `c` close an open picker, opening it without moving focus to its button first, removing the dropdown fix, and an earlier version of that fix which blocked typing into the Label filter. For the unit tests: dropping the picker's section, changing its description, not registering `c` at all, and for the dropdown, not marking the letter, marking it inside a search box too, marking it with Ctrl, marking a letter typed into an input inside the dropdown, and ignoring a search box inside the menu. Each break failed the matching test, and #56's and #58's tests stayed green.

**Not covered automatically, and why.** `c` doing nothing on an issue's own page, the compare page and a pull request's conversation tab was checked by hand, since there is no picker or create button there to declare it.

**Checked by hand.** Claude also drove a headless browser through a local instance: both lists signed in and out, an archived repository, and a real pull request's "Files changed" tab, where `c` and a mouse click gave the same focus steps through the arrow keys. It also typed into the Label filter on the list and the label picker on an issue, with and without the dropdown fix. I personally spot checked the features to ensure the features work as expected, such as on the issue list, in the filter, and on a pull request's "Files changed" tab.

| AC | What the tests check |
| --- | --- |
| AC1 | On the issue list, `c` goes to the new issue page, and to the template chooser once the repository has an issue template |
| AC2 | On the pull request list, `c` goes where "New Pull Request" leads |
| AC3 | Signed out, the greyed-out "New Pull Request" declares no `c`; in an archived repository neither list declares `c`, though "Compare commits" is shown |
| AC4 | On a real pull request's "Files changed" tab, `c` opens the picker with focus on its first entry, the arrow keys move within it, `c` again leaves it open, and Escape closes it and returns focus to its button, also while its commits are still loading |
| AC5 | On the issue list, `g c` goes to the front page instead of starting a new issue; `c` typed into the "Type" filter picks "Created by you" and starts no new issue |
| AC6 | "New Issue" and "New Pull Request" are in "Issues"; the mounted picker lists `c` as "Filter by commit" in "Pull Requests" |

## CI / manual verification

- CI runs on the PR; per the course rules, it must pass before merging.
- `make test-frontend`: 365 tests pass, including the 4 new ones.
- `make lint-js`, `make lint-templates` and `make lint-editorconfig` pass.
- The 13 Playwright tests in `tests/e2e/shortcut.test.ts` pass locally on Chromium and Firefox; each new one runs in under 1.5 s.
- `./.claude-students/check.sh` reports only the two `models-issues.md` size limits, which were failing before this PR.

## Design

Design decisions noted under issue #59.

## Tech Debt

**Introduced:**
- None.

**Encountered:**
- In the commit picker on "Files changed", ArrowDown from the first entry stops on the "hold Shift for a range" hint text before reaching the commits, because the picker's key handling focuses whatever element comes next. It does the same after a click, so `c` matches a click as AC4 asks; changing the picker is out of #59's scope. Not fixed here.

## Implementation Note
Despite the changes impacting the user-facing experience, there are no UI changes that require before and after screenshots. These shortcuts only take the user to another page or open the existing commit picker, and don't add, remove or change any element on the page.

## AI assistance

Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5) drafted the code, tests, docs and other changes, and ran the headless-browser checks and the checks that each test fails when its code is broken. I made the decisions, refused to let Claude commit on my behalf, and made commits as small as possible so I could review each one with its tests. AI-Log reference under related Issue #59.
```
</details></tool-use>

## Pull request format

Template: `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Title uses Conventional Commits, e.g.
`fix(issues): keep label filter after search`. Description sections:

1. `Closes #<N>`, which links the issue and closes it on merge. Every code PR links its issue, and
   the PR goes on the `Sprint 3` milestone too.
2. **What changed:** the change in your own words.
3. **Why:** the problem, and which acceptance criteria (AC1…) it satisfies.
4. **Test Evidence:** required from Sprint 3. It replaces the old "How it was tested" section.
   Every behaviour change still needs a new or updated test.

   ```markdown
   ## Test Evidence

   | Acceptance criterion | Test(s) | Level | Source of expected value |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | AC1: ... | ... | ... | ... |

   **Not tested automatically, and why:** [...]

   **AI-written tests:** [Which tests were written or modified by AI, and how you checked that their expected values are correct. If none, write "None."]
   ```

   - **One row per acceptance criterion** from the issue; for a bug report, the Expected Behavior.
     A PR that changes no product behaviour (e.g. a CI change) writes `N/A` and why.
   - **Test(s):** the test name, plus the file if not obvious. For a manual check, write `Manual:`
     followed by the steps and what you saw. An AC tested both ways lists both in the same row.
   - **Level:** `unit`, `integration`, `E2E` or `manual`.
   - **Source of expected value:** `AC`, `issue discussion`, `docs`, `upstream behavior`, or
     `other` (explain). **Never the current output of your own code:** a test whose expected value
     was copied from what the code returns cannot detect that the code is wrong.
   - **Not tested automatically, and why:** only for ACs checked manually only.
   - AI may draft this section; the author checks that it is accurate.

5. **CI / manual verification:** CI status. If CI doesn't run your tests, the commands you ran and
   a summary of the results (passed, failed, skipped).
6. **Design:** one line pointing at the Design Decision in the issue, or a note on how it changed.
7. **Tech Debt:** required from Sprint 2. Both fields are required, and `None.` is a valid answer:

   ```markdown
   ## Tech Debt
```

<!-- Title (for reference only, do not paste): feat(pull): block merging until dependency pull requests are merged -->

Closes #143

## What changed and why

A pull request that depends on another pull request could be merged as soon as that one was closed, even if it was never merged, so unfinished work could reach the target branch. This PR keeps it blocked until the pull requests it depends on are actually merged. Dependencies on issues work as before: closing the issue is enough.

- **Merging has its own dependency rule.** For merging, a dependency now counts as done only when it is a closed issue or a merged pull request. Closing keeps the old rule, where closed is enough, so a pull request whose dependency was closed without merging can still be closed.
- **All three ways of merging follow it.** The merge button, the API and a scheduled "merge when checks succeed" all pass through the same check before merging, so one change covers all three.
- **The merge button says why.** Pressing Merge shows "This pull request can't be merged until the pull requests it depends on are merged and the issues it depends on are closed." This is a new message: the old one, still shown when closing is blocked, only talks about closing issues.
- **The API refuses with 405 instead of 500.** It gives the same sentence, like its other reasons for refusing a merge. Before, an open dependency made it answer 500 Internal Server Error.
- **Turning dependencies off stops them from blocking merges.** With "Enable Dependencies For Issues and Pull Requests" off, dependencies are hidden and can't be removed, yet they still blocked the merge. The merge now ignores them, as closing already did.
- The docs in `.claude-students` describe how merging and closing check dependencies differently, and that fixture repositories have dependencies turned off.

## How the changes relate to the ACs

- **AC1:** Pressing Merge on B while A is closed without being merged shows the new message, and B is not merged.
- **AC2:** The API answers 405 Method Not Allowed with the same sentence, and B is not merged.
- **AC3:** A scheduled merge runs the same check when B's checks succeed, so B is not merged, stays open, and stays scheduled to be tried again on its next change.
- **AC4:** Once A is merged, B merges from the web and through the API as before.
- **AC5:** A dependency on an issue blocks while the issue is open and stops blocking once it is closed, as before.
- **AC6:** Closing B uses the closing rule, which treats A as done, so B closes as before.
- **AC7:** With dependencies turned off, the merge check skips them, so B merges.

| AC2: API answers 405 and does not merge | `tests/integration/pull_merge_dependency_test.go` › TestAPIMergePullBlockedByDependency; Manual: called the merge API on a local instance, got 405 with the sentence | integration, manual | AC (405, not merged); other: the message is design decision 3 |
| AC3: Scheduled merge does not go through | `tests/integration/pull_merge_dependency_test.go` › TestPullAutoMergeBlockedByDependency | integration | AC (not merged, stays open); other: "still scheduled" from the issue's Out of Scope ("tried again when its checks or reviews next change") |
| AC4: B merges once A is merged | `services/pull/check_test.go` › TestCheckPullMergeableDependencies/MergedPull; `models/issues/dependency_test.go` › TestMergeBlockedByDependencies/MergedPull; Manual: on a local instance, reopened and merged A, then merged one dependent pull request with the merge button and one through the API | unit, manual | AC |
| AC5: An open issue blocks, a closed one does not | `services/pull/check_test.go` › TestCheckPullMergeableDependencies/OpenIssue and /ClosedIssue; `models/issues/dependency_test.go` › TestMergeBlockedByDependencies/OpenIssue and /ClosedIssue | unit | AC |
| AC6: B can still be closed | `tests/integration/pull_merge_dependency_test.go` › TestPullCloseWithUnmergedDependency; `models/issues/dependency_test.go` › TestMergeBlockedByDependencies/PullClosedWithoutMerging (the closing rule) | integration, unit | AC; upstream behavior (the close request's response, from Gitea's existing close helper) |
| AC7: With dependencies off, B merges | `services/pull/check_test.go` › TestCheckPullMergeableDependencies/DependenciesTurnedOff; `tests/integration/pull_merge_dependency_test.go` › TestPullAutoMergeBlockedByDependency (its control really merges); Manual: on a local instance, a merge refused with dependencies on went through once they were turned off | unit, integration, manual | AC |

**Not tested automatically, and why:** None. Every AC has an automated test; the manual checks were done on top.

**AI-written tests:** All 14 new test cases (two Go unit tests with 5 cases each, and 4 integration tests) were written by Claude Code. I checked each expected value against the AC or other source it quotes, in a table per commit, and decided the 5 that needed interpreting: the closing rule standing in for AC6 at the unit level, AC7 at the check level, the web's HTTP 400, the API's message, and the scheduled merge staying scheduled.

**Why these levels.** The rule and the merge check are plain logic, so unit tests on the test database cover every row of the issue's table and the setting (AC4, AC5, AC7) without a server. Integration tests cover what only exists through a real request: the message the merge button gets (AC1), the API's status (AC2), the scheduled merge's queue (AC3) and closing through the page (AC6). They reuse the fixture pull requests instead of creating new ones, so each takes 0.1 to 0.2 s, except the scheduled merge test, which takes about 1 s because its control really merges.

**What "nothing happens" means here.** For AC3 the test waits for the merge queue to finish before checking that B was not merged, instead of checking right away. It then turns dependencies off and reports B's checks again, and B merges, which shows the first run was refused because of the dependency and was not simply skipped.

**Testing the tests.** Each test was checked by breaking the code it guards: for the rule, ignoring "merged" (the old rule), dropping issues from the query, ignoring "closed", turning its "or" into "and", and making the closing rule ask for "merged" too; for the merge check, ignoring the setting, inverting it, going back to the old rule, never returning the error, and a rule that only looks at pull requests; for the web and the API, the old message and leaving out the API's new case, which gave the 500 AC2 describes; for the scheduled merge, letting it ignore dependencies, and pointing it at the wrong commit so it never runs, where only the control failed, which is what the control is for. Each break failed the matching test, and the code was restored. [MUTATION RUN RESULT: filled in once the run ends]

```text
1	<!-- Title (for reference only, do not paste): feat(pull): block merging until dependency pull requests are merged -->
2	
3	Closes #143
4	
5	## What changed and why
6	
7	A pull request that depends on another pull request could be merged as soon as that one was closed, even if it was never merged, so unfinished work could reach the target branch. This PR keeps it blocked until the pull requests it depends on are actually merged. Dependencies on issues work as before: closing the issue is enough.
8	
9	- **Merging has its own dependency rule.** For merging, a dependency now counts as done only when it is a closed issue or a merged pull request. Closing keeps the old rule, where closed is enough, so a pull request whose dependency was closed without merging can still be closed.
10	- **All three ways of merging follow it.** The merge button, the API and a scheduled "merge when checks succeed" all pass through the same check before merging, so one change covers all three.
11	- **The merge button says why.** Pressing Merge shows "This pull request can't be merged until the pull requests it depends on are merged and the issues it depends on are closed." This is a new message: the old one, still shown when closing is blocked, only asks for issues to be closed.
12	- **The API refuses with 405 instead of 500.** It gives the same sentence, like its other reasons for refusing a merge. Before, an open dependency made it answer 500 Internal Server Error.
13	- **Turning dependencies off stops them from blocking merges.** With "Enable Dependencies For Issues and Pull Requests" off, dependencies are hidden and can't be removed, yet they still blocked the merge. The merge now ignores them, as closing already did.
14	- The docs in `.claude-students` describe how merging and closing check dependencies differently, and that fixture repositories have dependencies turned off.
15	
16	## How the changes relate to the ACs
17	
18	- **AC1:** Pressing Merge on B while A is closed without being merged shows the new message, and B is not merged.
19	- **AC2:** The API answers 405 Method Not Allowed with the same sentence, and B is not merged.
20	- **AC3:** A scheduled merge runs the same check when B's checks succeed, so B is not merged, stays open, and stays scheduled to be tried again on its next change.
21	- **AC4:** Once A is merged, B merges from the web and through the API as before.
22	- **AC5:** A dependency on an issue blocks while the issue is open and stops blocking once it is closed, as before.
23	- **AC6:** Closing B uses the closing rule, which treats A as done, so B closes as before.
24	- **AC7:** With dependencies turned off, the merge check skips them, so B merges.
25	
26	## Test Evidence
27	
28	| Acceptance criterion | Test(s) | Level | Source of expected value |
29	| --- | --- | --- | --- |

11. **go-mutesting traps found today:**
    - The "undefined: X" lines are noise from its old-style package lookup.
    - Diffs print *before* their `FAIL` line, and `PASS` lines have no diff.
    - Locations come from `report.json`'s `originalStartLine`.
    - `--no-exec` deletes its mutants unless `--do-not-remove-tmp-folder` is set.
    - Pointing `TMPDIR` elsewhere also catches compiler leftovers.
    - `--match` limits mutation to the named functions.
12. **Repo traps:**
    - `|` in a `make test-integration#…` name is run by the shell as a pipe; use `go test -tags '' -run 'A$|B$' gitea.dev/tests/integration` instead.
    - The repo-edit API ignores `internal_tracker` unless `has_issues` is sent with it.
    - Fixture repos have dependencies off.

422	     `go install github.com/avito-tech/go-mutesting/cmd/go-mutesting@latest`, with the Go from
423	     `go.mod` first on `PATH`. The binary lands in `~/go/bin`, which may need adding to `PATH`. For
424	     the write-up's Tool line, `go version -m "$(command -v go-mutesting)"` shows which version was
425	     installed.
426	   - Run it on the changed files only: `go-mutesting <changed .go files>`. Each mutant reruns all
427	     tests of that file's package.
428	   - It mutates whole files, not just the changed lines, and packages with database fixtures
429	     (`models/...`) are slow to test. Before the real run, time one `go test ./<pkg>/`, estimate the
430	     total, and tell the user.
431	   - Only package tests run. Behaviour covered only by `tests/integration/` will show up as
432	     survivors, so classify those honestly as unit-level test gaps, not as equivalent.
433	   - Save the terminal output as the `.txt` report. Its last line ("The mutation score is …") gives
434	     the score. Its PASS/FAIL wording is easy to misread (in its README, PASS means the mutant was
435	     killed), so go by the summary counts, and check one survivor by hand before classifying the rest.
436	   - If it can't load Gitea's packages (it's an older tool, and Gitea uses a recent Go), say so
437	     early. Item 10 says what to do when blocked.
438	4. **Known traps, both tools.** The tool first runs the selected tests on unchanged code and stops if
439	   any fail. Locally, `multiselect-aria.test.ts` already fails on untouched main, so leave it out if
```

## 1. Orientation

- Read `.claude-students/INDEX.md` first and only the 1–3 docs it maps to the task. They are
  "as accurate as they can be, but can be incorrect in the finer details" (ab-wm) — verify against code.
- Work backwards from the user-visible page: URL → route (`routers/web/web.go`) → handler → template
  (`templates/…`) → the element → the TypeScript that finds it (`web_src/js/…`).
- Frontend wiring: declarative `data-global-init="fnName"` + `registerGlobalInitFunc` (runs once per
  element, also for elements added later) is preferred over page-load `initXxx()` in `index.ts`.
  Fomantic-UI (jQuery) is deprecated: don't build new features on it, don't mix it with Vue.
- Gitea's HTML is an *input* to the TypeScript (rendered by Go templates, found with `querySelector`);
  the DOM is the state store. React intuitions mislead here — say so when explaining.
- Locale strings live only in `options/locale/locale_en-US.json` (JSON, not INI); other locales come
  from Crowdin. Prefer reusing an existing key when one already means the same thing.

  (`GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR="cp <todo>" git rebase -i <base>` with `exec git commit --amend -m …` lines) does
  it non-interactively — test it on a throwaway worktree first, and let the user run it on their branch.

  edit or commit until it ends, and check `git status` afterwards (an interrupted run can leave a
  mutant behind; `git restore` it). Don't run other tests of those packages while it runs.

```text
Dependency loops of three or more, and self-dependencies through the API, are accepted

## Observed Behavior
- On the web and through the API, a loop of three or more dependencies is accepted: # 1 depends on # 2 , # 2 on # 3, and # 3 on # 1. Only a loop of two is refused ("You cannot create a dependency with two issues that block each other."). None of the issues in such a loop can be closed, and none of the pull requests can be merged, until someone removes a dependency.
- Through the API, an issue or pull request can be made to depend on itself, after which it can never be closed or merged. The web refuses this with "You cannot make an issue depend on itself."
- Through the API, adding a dependency that already exists, or one that makes a loop of two, answers 500 Internal Server Error instead of saying what is wrong.

## Expected Behavior
- A dependency that would make a loop of any length is refused. On the web the message is "You cannot add this dependency, because the issues would block each other in a loop."
- A self-dependency is refused through the API, as it is on the web.
- The API answers 422 Unprocessable Entity for a loop or a self-dependency, and 409 Conflict for a dependency that already exists, as the close-reason endpoint does for invalid and conflicting requests.
- The same applies to both API endpoints that add a dependency, `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{index}/dependencies` and `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{index}/blocks`.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. In a repository with dependencies enabled, open issues # 1, # 2 and # 3.
2. On # 1, add # 2 as a dependency; on # 2, add # 3; on # 3, add # 1. All three are accepted.
3. Try to close any of the three: each is refused because of its open dependency.
4. Through the API, `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/1/dependencies` with `{"owner": "{owner}", "repo": "{repo}", "index": 1}`. Issue # 1 now depends on itself.
5. Send the same request with `"index": 2`. # 1 already depends on # 2 from step 2, and the API answers 500.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given # 1 depends on # 2 and # 2 on # 3, or # 1 depends on # 2 alone, when a user adds the dependency that closes the loop on the web, then it is refused with "You cannot add this dependency, because the issues would block each other in a loop." and nothing is added.
- [ ] AC2: Given the same, or # 1 depending on # 2 alone, when the dependency that closes the loop is added through the API, then the API answers 422 Unprocessable Entity and nothing is added.
- [ ] AC3: Given an issue or pull request, when it is added as its own dependency through the API, then the API answers 422 Unprocessable Entity and nothing is added.
- [ ] AC4: Given # 1 already depends on # 2, when the same dependency is added through the API, then the API answers 409 Conflict.
- [ ] AC5: Given dependencies that do not make a loop, such as # 1 and # 2 both depending on # 3, when they are added on the web or through the API, then they are accepted, as today.

## Additional Information
Found on `main` at `1410c7d404` while splitting #20. Once a pull request stays blocked until its dependencies are resolved (#143), a loop means none of its pull requests can ever be merged.

Evidence of the fix: each AC gets a test that fails on `main` and passes after the fix, listed in the PR's Test Evidence.

## Out of Scope
- Finding or removing loops that already exist.
- Which dependencies block closing or merging: Issue (#143)

## Design Decision
Added per commit during implementation, as in #53 and #54.

## Scope
small (2 points). Touches the check made when a dependency is added, and the API's answers to it; one rule widened from loops of two to loops of any length, plus three status codes and their tests.

## AI Disclosure
Used claude-code for the drafting of this issue, followed by my changes and proofing. Changes after the spec review were also made with claude-code.

Yes, #145 can be built from `main` without needing #143 or conflicting with it, as long as we avoid three specific spots.

**It doesn't depend on #143.** #145's ACs are all about *adding* a dependency: loops, self-dependencies, and the API's status codes. #143 only changes *merging*. The issue mentions #143 only as the reason loops matter more now. So #145 branches from `main`, and its tests won't need #143's rule.

**Where they meet, and how to avoid a conflict.** Git only conflicts when both branches change the same or neighbouring lines.

| File | #143 changed | #145 would change | Conflict? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `models/issues/dependency.go` | the import block, and a new function at the end | `CreateIssueDependency`, mid-file, for the loop check | No, unless #145 also edits the imports or the end of the file. I'd write the loop check without new imports. |
| `models/issues/dependency_test.go` | a `require` import, and a test at the end | new loop tests | Only if appended at the end. I'd put them next to the existing circular check in `TestCreateIssueDependency`, mid-file. |
| `options/locale/locale_en-US.json` | one key at line 1935 | the loop message, near line 1796 | No. The changes are far apart. |
| `routers/web/repo/issue_dependency.go`, `routers/api/v1/repo/issue_dependency.go`, the swagger file, `tests/integration/api_issue_dependency_test.go` | nothing | most of #145 | No |
| `.claude-students` docs | `services-pull-and-gitdiff.md`, `testing.md` and their guides, frontmatter included | possibly `models-issues.md` | Only if #145 edits the same two docs. Their `verified-at` lines would collide, so #145 stays out of them. |

If #145 merges first, #143 still merges cleanly. Just don't merge `main` into #143 after it's approved, because the course would then need a new approval.

**One decision: where to work.**
- (a) A new branch from `main` in this checkout, `fix/issue-145-dependency-loops`. To fix something on #143 during review, you `git switch` back between commits. The running server is unaffected either way, because it uses the binary that's already built.
- (b) A separate git worktree (a second checkout of the repo) in `.specstory/wt-145/`, so #143 stays checked out here. This avoids switching entirely. It costs a second checkout, and Go builds and tests there are slower the first time.

I recommend (a). #145 is small, has no frontend, and each commit leaves the tree clean, so switching back for a review fix is one command. Choose (b) if you expect #143's review to interrupt mid-commit.

Do you want to create the branch yourself, as you did for #143, or should I run `git switch -c fix/issue-145-dependency-loops origin/main`? It's local only and nothing gets pushed.

### Breaking PRs

#### What is a breaking PR?

A PR is breaking if it meets one of the following criteria:

- It changes API output in an incompatible way for existing users
- It removes a setting that an admin could previously set (i.e. via `app.ini`)
- An admin must do something manually to restore the old behavior

In particular, this means that adding new settings is not breaking.\
Changing the default value of a setting or replacing the setting with another one is breaking, however.

#### How to handle breaking PRs?

If your PR has a breaking change, you must add two things to the summary of your PR:

1. A reasoning why this breaking change is necessary
2. A `BREAKING` section explaining in simple terms (understandable for a typical user) how this PR affects users and how to mitigate these changes. This section can look for example like

```md
## :warning: BREAKING :warning:
```

Breaking PRs will not be merged as long as not both of these requirements are met.

AGENTS.md:11:- Use Conventional Commits for commit messages and PR titles, e.g. `type(scope): subject`, ending commit subjects with the issue number, e.g. `(#17)`; `!` before the colon if breaking. Use `test` type for test-only changes.
```
</details></tool-use>

## 1. Breaking change: title and description

**Title** (change it on GitHub): `feat(pull)!: block merging until dependency pull requests are merged`

**Description:** the local draft has a new `## :warning: BREAKING :warning:` section right after "What changed and why". Paste the whole body from `.specstory/issue-143-pr-description.md` again; the live body matched the draft before this change, so pasting it over loses none of your edits. The new section:

```markdown
## :warning: BREAKING :warning:

A pull request that was closed without being merged never put its work in the target branch, so the pull requests that depend on it must not be merged either; that is why merges that used to go through are now refused.

- **Some merges that used to go through are now refused.** While dependencies are turned on, a pull request that depends on a pull request closed without merging can no longer be merged, from the merge button, the API or a scheduled merge. To merge it, reopen and merge the pull request it depends on, or remove that dependency from the sidebar.
- **The merge API answers 405 instead of 500.** When dependencies block a merge, `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{index}/merge` now answers 405 Method Not Allowed with "This pull request can't be merged until the pull requests it depends on are merged and the issues it depends on are closed." instead of 500 Internal Server Error. Scripts should treat it like the endpoint's other 405 refusals: resolve the dependencies, then try again.
- **With dependencies turned off, they no longer block merging.** A pull request in such a repository used to be refused (the API answered 500) because of dependencies that were hidden and could not be removed; it now merges, as closing already ignored them.
```

- **Why it is breaking:** Gitea's `CONTRIBUTING.md` ("Breaking PRs") calls a PR breaking when it "changes API output in an incompatible way for existing users". It asks for a reason plus a `BREAKING` section in plain terms; the section's first sentence is the reason. CodeRabbit only mentioned the 405, but the bigger change for users is the merge that used to go through and now doesn't, so the first bullet covers that.
- **The commits keep their subjects.** AGENTS.md also wants the `!` on breaking commit subjects, but these commits are pushed, and adding it would need a force-push. The repo merges PRs with merge commits ("Merge pull request #142 …"), so the PR title is where the `!` shows.

## 2. Other issues on #146 (noted only)

1. **CodeRabbit check: "AI-written tests" doesn't name the tests.** Partly valid. "All 14 new test cases" does cover every new test, but the course template asks *which* tests. Naming the 6 test functions from the Test Evidence table would fix it in one sentence.
2. **CodeRabbit: the swagger docs say the 405 response is empty.** Valid in substance. The merge route documents 405 as `#/responses/empty`, but every 405 it returns, including the older ones, has a JSON message. Precedent is split: 3 routes use `empty` and 3 use `error`. The new BREAKING section now promises a message, so `empty` contradicts it.
   - The fix is one comment line, then `make generate-swagger`, which regenerates the swagger file, as a new commit.
   - It's partly pre-existing debt, so in scope or out is your call.
3. **CodeRabbit: the API message should be a locale key.** Wrong premise. The guideline it quotes ("never a literal") is from the *web* routes doc (`.claude-students/docs/routers-web.md:67`). In `routers/api/v1`, error messages are English literals: there are 8 literal 405 messages, and `ctx.Tr` is never used for an API error. That's also your decision 3. The reply is yours to write.

SonarQube Cloud's automatic analysis doesn't support code coverage, so projects that need coverage have to switch to CI-based analysis.

- **The limitation:** The official automatic analysis page lists coverage as a current gap, along with importing external rule engine reports. SonarQube Cloud can automatically analyze your code simply by reading it from your repository, without the need to configure a CI-based analysis.
- **Coverage is CI-only:** The coverage overview says the feature is only available for Overview of integrated CIs. It is not available for automatic analysis. SonarQube Cloud also does not calculate coverage itself, so you need a third-party tool that runs before the scanner step.
- **Switching over:** Per the language-specific guides, you go to **Administration > Analysis Method**, turn automatic analysis off, then under supported analysis methods pick your CI and follow the tutorial. Starting with an empty `sonar-project.properties` file before importing makes SonarQube Cloud set up CI-based analysis from the start.
- **Conflicts:** The two methods shouldn't run together. If you enable automatic analysis, you must ensure that you do not have any CI-based analyses configured. If you do then these CI-based analyses will fail and cause a failure in your build process.

The results are from several SonarSource docs pages, and the most recent pages were updated about two weeks ago. I didn't find any indication that coverage support under automatic analysis has been added.

Gitar's custom review instructions live in the repository's `.gitar/` folder, which has two main parts: review instructions and rules.

- **Review instructions (`.gitar/review/`):** Commit a markdown file under the **.gitar/review** directory. One file can pull in another with the @ syntax, so shared guidance lives in one place. Gitar's own repo uses an example file covering codebase conventions, such as which logging macro to use for operational visibility versus local debugging.
- **Rules (`.gitar/rules/*.md`):** Rules are defined as md files in .gitar/rules folder in your repository. Per the vendor's blog posts, these are written in natural language. One example from a third-party guide is a front-matter file with a `when` condition and `actions` to take, such as assigning a security team for auth-related PRs (Create workflow automation using .gitar/rules/*.md files with natural language descriptions). Those posts are marketing content, so verify the format against the official docs.
- **Approval criteria (`.gitar/config/`):** Drop a .gitar/config/approve.md file in any repo to set auto-approval rules for that codebase. Auto-apply limits work similarly through .gitar/config/apply.md.
- **Shared configuration:** Name one repository as your organization's configuration repository, and every other repository inherits its .gitar/ directory, and a repository's own copy of a skill or rule wins over the inherited one.
- **Other agent folders:** Gitar now reads repository instructions from .claude/rules alongside .cursor/rules and discovers skills in .agents/skills.

Gitar's documentation also says the setup is optional at first: Customize later with .gitar/ rules. The official code review page is at docs.gitar.ai/features/code-review, and the release notes are at docs.gitar.ai/release-notes.

Both of these are team-level chores, separate from #143. Here's what each would take.

## 4. Real coverage numbers in SonarQube

SonarQube Cloud only shows coverage when CI runs the tests with a coverage tool and sends it the report. The repo has no SonarQube workflow and no `sonar-project.properties`, so today it runs automatic analysis.

1. **Switch the analysis method** in SonarQube Cloud's Administration > Analysis Method, from Automatic to CI-based. This needs whoever administers the project there; I don't know who set it up. The two methods can't run at the same time: a CI scan fails while automatic analysis is on.
2. **Add a `SONAR_TOKEN` secret** to the GitHub repo, which needs a repo admin.
3. **Add a `sonar-project.properties` file** with the project key (`[REDACTED:generic-api-key]`, from the bot's links), the organization, which folders are code and which are tests, and `sonar.go.coverage.reportPaths=coverage.out`.
4. **Add a CI step that produces and uploads the report.** `make unit-test-coverage` already exists (`Makefile:421`) and writes `coverage.out`. A job runs it and then Sonar's scan action. To avoid running the unit tests twice, it could reuse the existing `test-unit` job in `pull-db-tests.yml` and pass the report along.

**Limits:**
- **Unit tests only:** this counts Go unit tests. Code that only integration tests reach, like our two handler branches, would still show as uncovered. Integration coverage is much heavier to wire up (`make coverage`, `Makefile:415`, across four databases).
- **Frontend coverage is separate:** it would also need a Vitest coverage package added to `package.json`, which isn't installed.

So: one small chore PR (a workflow plus a properties file), one secret, one admin setting. It's a team decision, because it changes everyone's CI.

## 5. Getting more out of Gitar

Its comment showed it ran with no rules and no issue-requirement checks.
- **Review instructions (documented on its code-review page):** markdown files under `.gitar/review/`, and one file can pull in another with `@`. A single file could point Gitar at the same sources your CodeRabbit config uses: the course's PR rules (Test Evidence, the AI section), `AGENTS.md`, and `CONTRIBUTING.md`'s breaking-PR rule. Then Gitar checks what your graders check.
- **Functional validation** (shown as "Not enabled" with a "Set up" link): it checks the PR "objective-by-objective" against the linked issue's requirements, so here #143's ACs. Its own docs say it judges the code and doesn't run tests. Setup is in Gitar's settings, and I don't know whether your plan includes it.
- **Review depth** (Focused or Thorough) is set per repo by an organization admin.
- **Approval criteria:** Gitar approves on criteria you define, so it could stop approving, which would avoid the "it says approved" confusion. That's described on its Auto-Approve page, which I haven't read.
- **Unverified leads:** search results also mention `.gitar/rules/*.md` and `.gitar/config/approve.md`, and that newer versions read `.claude/rules`. Those came from release notes and blog posts I didn't check, so confirm them against the docs before relying on them.

As with SonarQube, this would be its own chore PR on `main`, much like your CodeRabbit trial. Auto-apply stays off either way.

**Forked pull requests:** GitHub doesn't expose repository secrets to fork PR workflows, so a single build-and-analyze workflow can't run there. Automatic Analysis supports fork PRs but without coverage. For CI analysis with coverage, the page describes a three-workflow setup:

2. A workflow that builds fork code with no secrets and uploads artifacts.
3. A `workflow_run`-triggered workflow that checks out the fork's head SHA without running its code, then runs the scan with secrets.

The page warns to validate all values from fork PRs, pass them through `env:`, and keep permissions narrow.

The token and the switch-off are the only parts that need the professor. Below that are four design choices for you.

## What to ask the professor

1. **Add the token (can be done now; nothing uses it until the workflow merges).**
   - In SonarQube Cloud, create a token for the `csci-435-se` organization. Sonar's docs say: on the free plan, a personal access token; on a Team plan, an organization-scoped token.
   - Add it to `CSCI-435-SE/gitea` as a GitHub Actions secret named exactly `SONAR_TOKEN` (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret).
2. **Turn off Automatic Analysis, but only when the workflow PR is ready to test.**
   - Where: project `[REDACTED:generic-api-key]` → Administration → Analysis Method.
   - Why: Sonar's docs say a CI scan fails while automatic analysis is on, so the two can't overlap.
   - Side effect: after the switch, open PRs whose branch doesn't have the workflow yet get no Sonar result until they merge `main`.
3. **No impact for you:** GitHub doesn't give secrets to PRs from forks. The team works on branches in this repo, so that doesn't apply.

The project details are confirmed through SonarQube Cloud's public API: key `[REDACTED:generic-api-key]`, organization `csci-435-se`, public.

## Design choices

**1. Where the tests run for coverage**
- (a) The existing `test-unit` job (`pull-db-tests.yml`) also writes `coverage.out` on its first run and hands it to a new scan job. The unit tests still run once per PR.
- (b) A separate workflow that runs the unit tests again with coverage, then scans. It's easier to review or remove, but every backend PR runs the unit tests twice, and each run needs the same Elasticsearch, Redis, MinIO and other services.

I recommend (a).

**2. The scan of `main`.** Sonar compares each PR with the last scan of `main`, and today nothing runs on `main`.
- (a) A small workflow on each push to `main`: unit tests with coverage, then a scan. `main`'s dashboard then shows real coverage, at the cost of one test run per merge. GitHub doesn't charge public repos for Actions minutes.
- (b) A scan of `main` without coverage. It's fast, but `main`'s dashboard stays at 0%. As far as I know, PR comments would still show coverage of the new code, because that comes from the PR's own report. I haven't confirmed that in Sonar's docs.

I recommend (a). It's the only option where every number Sonar shows is real.

**3. Frontend coverage**
- (a) Go only for now.
- (b) Also TypeScript. That needs a Vitest coverage package added to `package.json` and the lockfile, which CodeRabbit's dependency check will ask a reason for.

I recommend (a), with (b) as a follow-up if wanted.

**4. PRs that skip the unit tests** (docs-only or frontend-only)
- (a) Scan anyway, without coverage, so every PR still gets a Sonar result, as it does today.
- (b) Skip the scan.

I recommend (a).

For the action itself, I'd pin `SonarSource/sonarqube-scan-action` v8.3.0 by its commit (`d209202…`), the way the repo pins every action. The newest release, v8.4.1, came out two days ago.

Answer as "1a 2a 3a 4a" or with your changes. You mentioned two things: tell me the second whenever you want.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-05 16:39:59Z)**_

Both facts check out:
- `@vitest/coverage-v8@4.1.9` exists, requires exactly `vitest 4.1.9`, and was published on 2026-06-15, so it's well established.
- The frontend tests take about 7 s locally (`make test-frontend`), so the scan job can simply rerun them.

## The design

- **Go coverage (1a):** in `test-unit`, the first `make test-backend` run also writes `coverage.out`, which is passed to the next job. The Go unit tests still run once.
- **The scan job:** a new `sonarqube` job in the same workflow, `pull-db-tests.yml`.
  - It runs for every PR, even when `test-unit` was skipped (4a).
  - It reruns the frontend tests with coverage, which takes seconds (3b).
  - It collects the Go report when there is one, then runs Sonar's scan.
  - The coverage options go in the workflow's command, so `vitest.config.ts`, your normal runs and Stryker stay unchanged.
- **The settings file:** `sonar-project.properties` holds the project key, the organization, which files are code and which are tests, and where both reports are.

## One more decision: where the `main` scan lives (2a)

- (i) **Add a push-to-`main` trigger to `pull-db-tests.yml`.** On a push, only `test-unit` and `sonarqube` run. The six database jobs get an extra condition, so they still run only on PRs. On a push `test-unit` always runs, so a docs-only merge can't replace `main`'s coverage with an empty scan. There's no duplication, but it touches the run condition (`if:`) of upstream jobs.
- (ii) **A separate workflow file for `main`** that copies `test-unit`'s setup, including the block of about 40 lines that starts Elasticsearch, Redis, MinIO and the rest, then runs both coverages and the scan. The upstream jobs stay untouched, but the copied block has to be kept in step with the original by hand.

I recommend (i). There's one definition of how the unit tests run, and the changes to upstream jobs are one condition each.

## Commit plan

1. `build(deps)`: add `@vitest/coverage-v8@4.1.9` as an exact dev dependency, changing `package.json` and `pnpm-lock.yaml`.
2. `build(sonar)`: add `sonar-project.properties`.
3. `ci(sonar)`: `test-unit` writes Go coverage, and the new `sonarqube` job scans PRs.
4. `ci(sonar)`: scan `main` after each merge, as you choose above.

**What I can check locally, and what I can't:**
- **Locally:** the workflow files with `make lint-actions`; the Go report's format on a few packages, including how its file paths look; and the frontend report.
- **Not locally:** the scan itself. It needs the token, and it can only run once the professor turns off Automatic Analysis. Until then, the PR's `sonarqube` job will fail, so it's best kept as a draft until both are done.

Answer (i) or (ii), and I'll start with commit 1.

The search didn't find documentation saying `go.mod` is used to resolve paths in `sonar.go.coverage.reportPaths`. The results point to a related problem: module-path mismatches cause coverage to be dropped.

- **Official docs:** SonarQube Cloud's Go guidance says the property must point to the report file your coverage tool writes, and wildcards and comma-separated lists are supported. It is set in the sonar-project.properties file, located in the project root. It doesn't mention `go.mod` at all.
- **Module-path mismatch:** In one forum thread, a user with a `go.mod` in a subdirectory found that SonarCloud read file paths as a file located in the mod_a/b/c/x.go (relative to the repository root), so coverage for those files was ignored. The user asked whether pointing `sonar.projectBaseDir` at the module root would help, and the thread doesn't show an answer.
- **Path format:** A Sonar staff reply in another thread says coverage report should either contain absolute paths or paths relative to a project base directory. A user fixed this by rewriting the paths in `coverage.out` before running the scanner.
- **Monorepo:** In a monorepo thread, a user with multiple `go.mod` files ran the scan with -Dsonar.go.coverage.reportPaths="**/coverage.out". That is a wildcard, not a `go.mod` lookup, and the thread doesn't say whether it worked.

Practical takeaway: check that the module path in `go.mod` matches the import paths in `coverage.out`, and that the file paths in the report are relative to the analysis base directory. Nothing I found confirms that SonarQube reads `go.mod` directly.

**What changed and why** (all in `.github/workflows/pull-db-tests.yml`)

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-05 17:06:57Z)**_

No. The token must not go in any file. The repo is public, so a token in a file would be readable by anyone and would stay in the git history even after you deleted it.

The PR already does its part. The workflow reads the token from GitHub's secret store at `.github/workflows/pull-db-tests.yml:288`:

```yaml
        env:
          SONAR_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SONAR_TOKEN }}
```

That's the only place it's referenced; `sonar-project.properties` needs no token. So once the secret exists, no file changes are needed.

**What the professor does:**
1. **Create the token** in SonarQube Cloud for the `csci-435-se` organization.
2. **Add it to GitHub:** `CSCI-435-SE/gitea` → Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret.
   - **Name:** exactly `SONAR_TOKEN`.
   - **Value:** the token.
   - An organization-level secret with the same name also works, as long as this repo is allowed to use it.
3. **When you're ready to test:** turn off Automatic Analysis for project `[REDACTED:generic-api-key]` (Administration → Analysis Method).

**Then, to see it run:** re-run the PR's `db-tests` workflow, or push any commit. Secrets are read when a run starts, so runs from before the secret existed won't pick it up.

On "it should just work": the parts I could check locally pass. The workflow linters pass, the Go and TypeScript reports are written, and every path in the Go report points to a real file. The scan itself has never run, because it can't without the token. The first real run is where any problem would show, for example Sonar not matching the coverage paths. If it fails, its log will say why and we fix it from there.

Commit 4 landed (`d8e499cbec`). Next on my side is the PR description, unless you want the optional docs line first.

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://coderabbit.ai/integrations/schema.v2.json
# CodeRabbit settings for the CSCI 435 fork; every key is in https://docs.coderabbit.ai/reference/configuration
# Reviews treat each PR as if it were going upstream to go-gitea/gitea; where the course rules differ, they win.
language: en-US
tone_instructions: "Review like a Gitea maintainer helping a student team with little time. Raise real bugs, security holes, unmet acceptance criteria and broken repo rules. Start each comment with Required or Optional. Be brief: no praise or style nits."

reviews:
  profile: chill
  high_level_summary: false # PR descriptions are graded, so the bot must not write into them
  sequence_diagrams: false
  estimate_code_review_effort: false
  related_issues: false
  related_prs: false
  suggested_labels: false
  suggested_reviewers: false
  in_progress_fortune: false
  enable_prompt_for_ai_agents: false
  auto_review:
    auto_incremental_review: false # one review when the PR leaves draft; comment "@coderabbitai review" for another
  path_filters:
    - "!ai-logs/**" # course logs are filed unedited
    - "!.claude-students/guide/**" # generated from .claude-students/docs
    - "!docs/superpowers/**" # AI planning notes
    - "!docs/sprint3/mutation/reports/**" # raw mutation tool output for D6
    - "!templates/swagger/v1_json.tmpl" # generated, and CI checks it is up to date
    - "!templates/swagger/v1_openapi3_json.tmpl"
    - "!web_src/fomantic/build/**" # vendored
  path_instructions:
    - path: "**"
      instructions: |
        The project rules are AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, docs/sprint0/standards.md, docs/guidelines-backend.md, docs/guidelines-frontend.md, and the .claude-students/docs page that .claude-students/INDEX.md maps to the changed path. Cite the rule when you raise one.
        Course rules win where they differ from upstream: PRs here are merged with a merge commit, and AI logs and .claude-students docs are committed on purpose.
        - Scope: a PR covers one issue. Flag changes unrelated to the linked issue (CONTRIBUTING.md: "Don't make changes unrelated to your PR").
        - Layers: imports flow cmd → routers → services → models → modules only. Flag an import against that direction.
        - Comments: short, explaining why, never narrating the code. Flag a removed comment that is still true. Never ask for docstrings.
        - Docs drift: if the change makes a statement in a .claude-students/docs page wrong, ask for that page to be fixed in the same PR (AGENTS.md).
        - Commits: a commit made with AI help, including one pushed by a bot, ends with an `Assisted-by: AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION` trailer, and no commit carries `Co-Authored-By` or `Signed-off-by` (AGENTS.md, .claude-students/COURSE-WORKFLOW.md). If possible, the message also names the person who approved the change, since a human approves every commit.
        - Skipped tests and disabled checks: a newly skipped test (`t.Skip`, `it.skip`, `test.skip`, `test.fixme` and the like) or a disabled CI check or workflow job needs a linked issue and a reason in a code comment (AGENTS.md; Sprint 3, D8).
        - Skip anything `make fmt`, `make lint-go`, `make lint-js`, `make lint-css` or `make lint-templates` enforces; CI runs them.
    - path: "**/*.go"
      instructions: |
        - A new .go file starts with `// Copyright <current year> The Gitea Authors. All rights reserved.` and `// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT`.
        - Writes that must roll back together run inside `db.WithTx` or `db.WithTx2`, and every function in the transaction takes `context.Context` first.
        - XORM: flag an `Update` or `Delete` with no `Where` or ID condition; it touches every row.
        - Before reading or changing another user's or repository's data, the doer's permission is checked. Treat a missing check as a security bug.
        - Handlers fail through the context helpers (`ctx.NotFound`, `ctx.ServerError`, `ctx.JSONError` and the like), never by writing the response by hand.
        - User-visible text is a locale key, never a literal; user-facing errors go through `util.ErrorWrapTranslatable`.
        - `go.mod` and `go.sum` change only when the feature needs it, after `make tidy`.

        - Cover the normal case, invalid input and permission checks where they apply (docs/sprint0/standards.md).
        - Integration tests should run in under 2 seconds. Don't ask for tests beyond what the acceptance criteria need.

build(mutation-testing): installed and setup foundations for mutation testing tools
----
<!-- Title (reference only, don't paste this line): chore(mutation): set up StrykerJS and go-mutesting for mutation testing -->

## What changed and Why

Set up the repo for Sprint 3 mutation testing (D6), so everyone can run the tools on their own files.

- StrykerJS and its Vitest runner added as dev dependencies, with a shared config (`stryker.config.mjs`) that names no files: you pass them with `--mutate`.
- A Stryker-only Vitest config (`stryker.vitest.config.ts`) that turns test isolation on. Without it Stryker can't start on some files (see Tech Debt).
- go-mutesting for the Go side. Gremlins was not used/tested as per their own docs: "Gremlins doesn't work very well on very big Go modules, mainly because a run can take hours to complete".
- `.gitignore` entries for Stryker's sandbox and reports, and the `report.json` go-mutesting always writes.
- A new `.claude-students` page and guide on running both tools and their pitfalls, linked from `INDEX.md` and the D6 section.
- My own Stryker config in `docs/sprint3/mutation/`

## Test Evidence

| Acceptance criterion | Test(s) | Level | Source of expected value |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| N/A: tooling and docs only, no product behaviour changes | N/A | N/A | N/A |

**Not tested automatically, and why:** N/A

**AI-written tests:** None.

## CI / manual verification

CI Passed.

Manually checked by running Styker on shortcut.ts within Modules, which uncovered surviving mutants for a 84.15% score. go-mutestring was also tested on paginate.go with surviving mutants (60%). Eslint passed, along with other lint checks.


## Design

- One shared config, plus personal configs that import it, with the files passed on the command line, so no config is tied to one issue
- Stryker's sandbox copy skips everything in `.gitignore`
- go-mutesting over Gremlins, and no go-mutesting config file, since the JSON report it would turn on is always written anyway

## Tech Debt

**Introduced:** `stryker.vitest.config.ts` works around an order-dependent test instead of fixing it. A hardening issue will follow. go-mutesting is installed from `@master`, not a pinned version, because its v2 tags can't be installed by version number.

**Encountered:** `repo-issue-edit.test.ts` fails when it shares a worker with `shortcut.test.ts`, which is what Stryker does, because the repo's Vitest config has `isolate: false`. It fails the same way in plain Vitest with `--no-file-parallelism`. Personal `.mjs` configs under `docs/` aren't covered by `make lint-js`.

## AI assistance

Set up, configured and tested by Claude Code (Opus 5.5), including the trial runs and the docs. Verified by me, along with the manual checks stated in the "manual verification" section.
