```text
<!-- markdownlint-disable MD029 -->
<!-- Rules are numbered continuously 1-15 across the sections below; check.sh error
     messages and all 34 docs cite them by number, so the sequence must not restart. -->

# Maintenance rules

Five people maintain one shared set of docs. These rules exist so the set stays *one* set. Read
them before editing anything in `.claude-students/`. Rules marked **[checked]** are enforced by
`./.claude-students/check.sh`.

## Scope discipline

1. **Upstream wins.** `AGENTS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `docs/guidelines-*.md` are authoritative.
   Docs here summarise them and link to them; they never restate a rule differently and never
   contradict one. A contradiction is a bug in this folder, not in the project.
2. **One fact, one home.** Every fact lives in exactly one doc — the one whose `scope:` owns that
   path. Everywhere else, link to it. Duplicated facts are how five maintainers end up with five
   different answers.
3. **Durability test.** Record a fact only if it (a) took more than one discovery step to find and
   (b) will still be true after the next upstream merge. A one-off workaround, a sprint detail or
   anything about your own task fails this test — that belongs in `ai-logs/`.
4. **No process notes.** No TODOs, no open questions, no first person, no student names, no dates
   other than `verified-at`. This is a map of the code, not a journal.

## Form

5. **Template only [checked].** Use the `## ` headings from `_TEMPLATE.md`, all of them, in that
   order, with nothing added. If a section has nothing to say, write one line saying so.
6. **120-line cap [checked].** Going over means the scope is too broad. Split the doc, and add the
   new `INDEX.md` row in the same commit. `INDEX.md` itself is capped at 60 lines.
7. **Cite or delete [checked, partially].** Every claim names a repo path. A claim with no path is
   unverifiable by the next reader — delete it.
8. **Symbols, not line numbers [checked].** Write `models/db/context.go` → `WithTx`, never
   `models/db/context.go:143`. Line numbers rot at the next upstream merge and a stale number is
   worse than no number. Code fences stay at 10 lines or fewer — point at the file instead of
   copying it.
9. **Repo-relative paths [checked].** `models/db/context.go`, never `/home/you/gitea/models/...`.
10. **Whitespace [checked].** No trailing whitespace, LF endings, final newline — same as the rest
    of the repo (`.editorconfig`).

## Change control

11. **One universal set.** These docs live on `main` and nowhere else. Never keep a personal copy,
    a per-student folder, or a long-lived branch of them.
12. **Changes land by PR**, titled `docs(context): <subject>` per `AGENTS.md` Conventional Commits,
    with an `Assisted-by: AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION` trailer and no `Co-Authored-By` or
    `Signed-off-by`.
13. **Fix in place.** If you discover while working that a doc is wrong or incomplete, correct it
    in the *same* PR as your code change and update `verified-at` to the commit you checked
    against. Leaving a doc stale for someone else to hit is the exact failure this folder exists to
    prevent. This rule applies to AI sessions too.
14. **New docs need three things in one commit [checked]:** the file, its `INDEX.md` row, and a
    `scope:` that does not overlap any existing doc's. If the scope overlaps, you wanted to edit
    that doc, not add one.
15. **`./.claude-students/check.sh` passes before you push [checked].** It is dependency-free and
    finishes in under a second.

## The guide layer (rules 16-22)

`guide/` holds a plain-English page for each reference page in `docs/`, same filename. It exists so
a person new to Go and to this codebase can get oriented. It is **derived**, not independent.

16. Every guide carries `source:`, `source-hash:` and `verified-at:` in its frontmatter **[checked]**.
17. A guide's `source:` names a real `docs/*.md` with the **same filename** **[checked]**.
18. `source-hash:` is the first 16 characters of `sha256sum docs/<name>.md`. If the reference page
    changes and the guide is not regenerated, `check.sh` reports **drift** **[checked]**. Regenerating
    means: reread the reference page, rewrite the guide, update the hash and `verified-at`.
19. Guide headings match `guide/_TEMPLATE.md` exactly and in order **[checked]**.
20. Guides are capped at **200 lines**, code fences at **30** **[checked]** — teaching needs more room
    than reference does.
21. **A guide adds explanation, vocabulary and worked steps. It adds no new facts.** Every repo path
    a guide cites must also be cited by its source page **[checked]**. If you need a fact the
    reference page lacks, add it *there* first, which bumps the hash and forces the guide to be
    regenerated in the same commit — exactly the intended order.
22. `guide/START-HERE.md` has no source page. It is exempt from rules 17, 18 and 21, and is where
    cross-cutting material lives that no single reference page owns.

**Never fix a fact in `guide/`.** If the two layers disagree, the reference page is the truth and
the guide is stale: fix `docs/`, regenerate the guide, ship both in one PR. A disagreement is a bug
report against `docs/`, not an editing job in `guide/`.

**Known limitation:** a hand-edit to a guide that only rewords prose is not mechanically
detectable. Rule 21 catches invented facts; rule 18 catches a stale guide; review catches the rest.

## Updating `verified-at`

`verified-at` is the short SHA the doc was last checked against, from `git rev-parse --short HEAD`.
Bump it whenever you confirm or correct a doc. A doc whose `verified-at` is far behind `main` has
not been checked recently — treat its details as hints and confirm them in the code before relying
on them.

23:  dependencies to a minimum
24-  - `models/db`: core database operations
25-  - `models/fixtures`: sample data used by tests
26-  - `models/migrations`: schema migration scripts
27:- `modules`: standalone functionality with few dependencies
28-  - `modules/setting`: configuration handling
29-  - `modules/git`: interaction with the Git command line
30-- `routers`: request handlers, split into `api`, `web`, `install`, and `private`
31-- `services`: business logic that ties routers and models together
32-- `templates`: Go HTML templates
33-- `public`: compiled frontend assets
34-- `tests`: integration and end-to-end test helpers
35-
36:### Dependency direction
37-
38:Dependencies only flow in one direction:
39-
40-```text
41-cmd → routers → services → models → modules
42-```
43-
44-A package on the left may import a package on its right, but never the reverse.
45-
46-### Naming conventions
47-
48-- Top-level packages use the plural form: `services`, `models`, `routers`.
49-- Subpackages use the singular form: `services/user`, `models/repository`.
50-
--
74:## Dependencies
75-
76:Go dependencies are managed with [Go Modules](https://go.dev/ref/mod).
77-
78-Pull requests should only modify `go.mod` and `go.sum` where it relates to the
79-change at hand, be it a bug fix or a new feature. Otherwise, these files should only
80:be touched by pull requests whose sole purpose is updating dependencies. Run
81-`make tidy` after any change to `go.mod`.
82-
83-Any `go.mod` / `go.sum` update must be justified in the PR description and must be
84-verified by reviewers and the merger to reference an existing upstream commit.
85-
86-## API v1
87-
88-The API is documented with [Swagger](https://gitea.com/api/swagger) and is modelled
89-on [the GitHub API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest).
90-
91-### GitHub API compatibility
92-
----
180-Use one of these types:
181-
182:- `build`: Changes affecting the build system, packaging, or external dependencies
183-- `ci`: Changes to CI/CD configuration files and scripts
184-- `chore`: Maintenance changes that do not affect production code or should not appear in the changelog
185-- `docs`: Documentation-only changes
186-- `feat`: A larger user-facing feature, improvement, or new functionality
187-- `enhance`: Small or trivial user-facing improvements or UX polish (for example wording changes, color adjustments, spacing or padding tweaks, placeholders, small UI behavior improvements)
188:- `fix`: A bug fix, UX correction, or security-related dependency update
189-- `perf`: Performance improvements (speed, memory, scalability)
190-- `refactor`: A code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature
191-- `revert`: Reverts a previous change
192-- `style`: Formatting or style-only changes that do not affect code behavior (for example lint-driven edits)
193-- `test`: Adding or correcting tests
194-
195-Examples:
196-
197-```text
198-fix(web): prevent avatar upload crash on empty file
199-feat(api): add pagination to repo hooks list
200-enhance(repo): improve diff toolbar spacing
```

<!-- Title (reference only, don't paste this line): ci(sonar): run SonarQube Cloud from CI with Go and TypeScript coverage -->

## What changed and Why

SonarQube Cloud runs its automatic analysis here, which only reads the code, so every pull request shows "0.0% Coverage on New Code" whatever its tests do: SonarQube's docs say automatic analysis doesn't support coverage. This PR moves the project to CI-based analysis, so SonarQube gets real coverage from our own test runs.

- **`sonar-project.properties`** names the project (`[REDACTED:generic-api-key]` in the `csci-435-se` organization), marks test files as tests so they don't count as code that needs coverage, and points at the two coverage reports.
- **Go coverage comes from the existing `test-unit` run**, not a second one: its first `make test-backend` writes `coverage.out` and hands it to the new `sonarqube` job. Go writes the paths as `gitea.dev/...`, so they are rewritten to repository paths, which SonarQube expects.
- **A new `sonarqube` job** runs the frontend tests with coverage (about 8 s locally) and scans. It runs for every pull request from this repository, including ones that don't touch the backend (then without Go coverage), and skips pull requests from forks, which GitHub gives no secrets.
- **Merges to `main` are scanned too**, so SonarQube has a `main` to compare pull requests with. After a merge only `test-unit` and `sonarqube` run; the database jobs stay pull-request only.
- **`@vitest/coverage-v8` 4.1.9 is a new dev dependency**: Vitest needs it to measure coverage, and its version must match Vitest's (4.1.9). pnpm also moved two existing indirect versions within their allowed ranges, to versions the lockfile already had: `@babel/parser` 8.0.10 → 8.1.0 inside four Babel packages, and `@jridgewell/sourcemap-codec` 1.5.5 → 1.6.0. `/coverage`, where Vitest writes its report, is gitignored.
- The `.claude-students` build-and-tooling page and its guide describe the setup, and why the `sonarqube` job can fail.

## Before merging (needs a repository admin)

1. Add a repository secret named `SONAR_TOKEN` (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions) holding a SonarQube Cloud token for the `csci-435-se` organization. No file in this PR holds the token; the workflow reads it from the secret.
2. In SonarQube Cloud, project `[REDACTED:generic-api-key]` → Administration → Analysis Method, turn off Automatic Analysis. A scan from CI fails while it is on.

Until both are done, this PR's `sonarqube` job fails, so the PR stays a draft. After step 2, open pull requests that don't include this workflow get no SonarQube result until they merge `main`.

## Test Evidence

| Acceptance criterion | Test(s) | Level | Source of expected value |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| N/A: CI configuration, tooling and docs only, no product behaviour changes | N/A | N/A | N/A |

**Not tested automatically, and why:** N/A

**AI-written tests:** None.

## CI / manual verification

- The workflow linters pass: `make lint-actions` (actionlint, and zizmor with no findings), `make lint-yaml` and `make lint-editorconfig`.
- The Go half was rehearsed locally: `make test-backend` with the new flags on `modules/util` and `models/issues` wrote the report, all 58 paths in it point to real files after the rewrite, and `make test-check` still passes with the report present (it is gitignored, like the output of upstream's `make unit-test-coverage`).
- The frontend half was rehearsed locally: the job's Vitest command passed all 388 tests and wrote only `coverage/lcov.info`, with every path under `web_src/js/`.
- With the new dependency, `CI=true pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `make test-frontend`, `make lint-js` and `make frontend` pass.
- `./.claude-students/check.sh` passes.
- Not verified yet: the scan itself, which needs the two steps above. Its first run on this PR shows whether SonarQube reads both reports.

## Design

- Coverage comes from the existing `test-unit` run rather than running the unit tests twice; they need Elasticsearch, Redis, MinIO and other services.
- Scanning `main` is a push trigger on `pull-db-tests.yml`, with the database jobs limited to pull requests, rather than a separate workflow copying `test-unit`'s service setup.
- Every pull request is scanned, with Go coverage only when the backend tests ran; the frontend tests are cheap enough to rerun in the scan job.
- Actions are pinned by commit like the rest of the repository, to releases at least four weeks old: the scan action v8.3.0, `upload-artifact` v7.0.2 and `download-artifact` v8.0.2.

## Tech Debt

**Introduced:**
- Go coverage counts unit tests only. Code reached only through `tests/integration`, which is most HTTP handlers, still shows as uncovered; collecting integration coverage (`make coverage`) across four databases is a bigger change.
- The path rewrite names the Go module (`gitea.dev`), so renaming the module means updating that step.

**Encountered:**
- SonarQube's docs don't say whether it can read Go's module paths in `coverage.out`, so the paths are rewritten before the scan instead of relying on it.

## AI assistance

Verified by me, and every commit was made by me.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-05 17:17:49Z)**_

Gitar found a real bug, and the fix is staged and ready for you to commit.

**The bug:** GitHub Actions silently adds `success()` to any step condition that has no status function. So the Go-coverage download (`pull-db-tests.yml:281`) was skipped whenever the frontend tests failed. The scan still ran, because it has `!cancelled()`, but with no Go report. That would have shown 0% Go coverage, and on `main` it would have recorded a wrong baseline. My comment on the scan step promised only the frontend coverage would be lost in that case. The CI reviewer read the case the same way I did, so neither of us caught it.

**The fix:** the download step's condition is now `${{ !cancelled() && needs.test-unit.result == 'success' }}`, with a short comment saying why. That's Gitar's suggested change, made as a normal commit.

**Checks:**
- actionlint and zizmor ("No findings"), yamllint, editorconfig and the whitespace check pass.
- I can't reproduce the failure case on CI without breaking a frontend test, so this rests on the documented `success()` rule, which I checked before agreeing with Gitar.

**CI on #147 so far:** 8 passed, 6 still running, 12 skipped, and 1 failed, `sonarqube`, as expected. Its annotations say "Running this GitHub Action without SONAR_TOKEN is not recommended", and the scanner exited with code 3. One useful confirmation: `frontend-coverage` passed on GitHub, so the Vitest coverage run works in CI.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-11-05 17:30:08Z)**_

Both CodeRabbit findings hold up against the code.

**1. A tested file is left out of the frontend coverage.** Valid.
- **Why:** Vitest runs tests in two places, `web_src/**/*.test.ts` and `tools/eslint-rules/**/*.test.ts` (`vitest.config.ts:7-10`), and `tools/eslint-rules/unescaped-html-literal.test.ts` really exists. The job only collects coverage for `web_src/js/**`, so `unescaped-html-literal.ts` is tested but reported as uncovered.
- **Fix:** add `tools/eslint-rules/**` to the coverage scope in the `frontend-coverage` step, so it matches where Vitest's tests live. I'd confirm locally that the file then shows up in `lcov.info`.
- **Not part of the finding, just noting it:** other TypeScript lies outside both folders, such as the root config files (`vite.config.ts`, `eslint.config.ts`, …), the `tools/*.ts` generators and the vendored `web_src/fomantic/build/*.js`. No unit tests cover these, by design. Sonar *may* count them as uncovered in its overall number; I haven't confirmed how it treats files missing from the report. A `sonar.coverage.exclusions` line could leave them out, but that's beyond what CodeRabbit raised, so it's your call. I'd leave it until the first real scan shows whether it matters.

**2. Go coverage is dropped when a later `test-unit` step fails.** Valid. It's the same kind of bug Gitar found, one layer up.
- **Why:** the Go report is uploaded right after the first test run, but the job still continues with `unit-tests-gogit` and `make test-check`. If either of those fails, the job counts as failed, so `needs.test-unit.result == 'success'` is false. The download is skipped even though a complete report was uploaded, and on `main` that would again record a wrong baseline.
- **Fix:** download whenever `test-unit` ran, with the condition `${{ !cancelled() && needs.test-unit.result != 'skipped' }}`. Mark the step `continue-on-error: true`, because the report is missing when the first test run itself failed, and `download-artifact` fails if there's nothing to download. The scan then goes ahead without Go coverage.

**The heading check** (`What changed` / `Why` as separate sections): that's your usual pushback, and #141 and #143 use the combined heading. The reply is yours to write.

**How to commit them:** two small commits, one per finding, or one bundled review-fix commit. Which do you want? I'll make both changes and run the workflow linters either way.

< ## What changed and Why
---
> SonarQube Cloud runs its automatic analysis here, which only reads the code, so every pull request shows "0.0% Coverage on New Code" whatever its tests do: SonarQube's docs say automatic analysis doesn't support coverage. This PR moves the project to CI-based analysis, so SonarQube gets real coverage from our own test runs.
> 
> - **`sonar-project.properties`** names the project (`[REDACTED:generic-api-key]` in the `csci-435-se` organization), marks test files as tests so they don't count as code that needs coverage, and points at the two coverage reports.
> - **Go coverage comes from the existing `test-unit` run**, not a second one: its first `make test-backend` writes `coverage.out` and hands it to the new `sonarqube` job. Go writes the paths as `gitea.dev/...`, so they are rewritten to repository paths, which SonarQube expects.
> - **A new `sonarqube` job** runs the frontend tests with coverage (about 8 s locally) and scans. It runs for every pull request from this repository, including ones that don't touch the backend (then without Go coverage), and skips pull requests from forks, which GitHub gives no secrets.
> - **Merges to `main` are scanned too**, so SonarQube has a `main` to compare pull requests with. After a merge only `files-changed`, `test-unit` and `sonarqube` run; the database jobs stay pull-request only.
> - **`@vitest/coverage-v8` 4.1.9 is a new dev dependency**: Vitest needs it to measure coverage, and its version must match Vitest's (4.1.9). pnpm also moved two existing indirect versions within their allowed ranges, to versions the lockfile already had: `@babel/parser` 8.0.10 → 8.1.0 inside four Babel packages, and `@jridgewell/sourcemap-codec` 1.5.5 → 1.6.0. `/coverage`, where Vitest writes its report, is gitignored.
> - The `.claude-students` build-and-tooling page and its guide describe the setup, and why the `sonarqube` job can fail.
> 
> ## Before merging (needs a repository admin)
> 
> 1. Add a repository secret named `SONAR_TOKEN` (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions) holding a SonarQube Cloud token for the `csci-435-se` organization. No file in this PR holds the token; the workflow reads it from the secret.
> 2. In SonarQube Cloud, project `[REDACTED:generic-api-key]` → Administration → Analysis Method, turn off Automatic Analysis. A scan from CI fails while it is on.
> 
> Until both are done, this PR's `sonarqube` job fails, so the PR stays a draft. After step 2, open pull requests that don't include this workflow get no SonarQube result until they merge `main`.
>

>

> | --- | --- | --- | --- |
> | N/A: CI configuration, tooling and docs only, no product behaviour changes | N/A | N/A | N/A |
> 
> **Not tested automatically, and why:** N/A
> 
> **AI-written tests:** None.
> 
> ## CI / manual verification
> 
> - The workflow linters pass: `make lint-actions` (actionlint, and zizmor with no findings), `make lint-yaml` and `make lint-editorconfig`.
> - The Go half was rehearsed locally: `make test-backend` with the new flags on `modules/util` and `models/issues` wrote the report, all 58 paths in it point to real files after the rewrite, and `make test-check` still passes with the report present (it is gitignored, like the output of upstream's `make unit-test-coverage`).
> - The frontend half was rehearsed locally: the job's Vitest command passed all 388 tests and wrote only `coverage/lcov.info`, with every path under `web_src/js/`.
> - With the new dependency, `CI=true pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `make test-frontend`, `make lint-js` and `make frontend` pass.
> - `./.claude-students/check.sh` passes.
> - Not verified yet: the scan itself, which needs the two steps above. Its first run on this PR shows whether SonarQube reads both reports.
> 
> ## Design
> 
> - Coverage comes from the existing `test-unit` run rather than running the unit tests twice; they need Elasticsearch, Redis, MinIO and other services.
> - Scanning `main` is a push trigger on `pull-db-tests.yml`, with the database jobs limited to pull requests, rather than a separate workflow copying `test-unit`'s service setup.

# Code Review

> Review code behavior with AST-informed context, team knowledge, and checks across repositories

## Overview

Gitar reviews PRs using the surrounding code and the team's engineering context. Findings land on the changed lines, with explanations and suggested fixes.

> [card] Security Analysis
>
> Vulnerabilities, unsafe patterns, input validation

> [card] Bug Detection
>
> Logic errors, null pointer risks, edge cases

> [card] Performance
>
> Algorithm complexity, database queries, memory usage

> [card] Code Quality
>
> Readability, maintainability, best practices

## Beyond the changed lines

Gitar uses [AST-informed code structure](https://docs.gitar.ai/how-gitar-works.md#code-structure-informs-the-review) to navigate the implementation, then reads related files and searches for callers to investigate the effect of a change.

| Coverage | What it adds to the review |
| - | - |
| [Agentic Security](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/agentic-security.md) | Security review of changes to agent instructions and supporting scripts. |
| [Knowledge](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/knowledge.md) | Team conventions learned from instructions and human review feedback, with source citations. |
| [Cross-Repo Analysis](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/cross-repo-analysis.md) | Impacts on other repositories, including dependencies across code hosts. |
| [Cross-PR Analysis](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/cross-pr-analysis.md) | Logic mismatches between related open PRs, with references to both changes. |
| [Functional Validation](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/functional-validation.md) | Objective-by-objective checks against linked issue requirements. |
| [Risk Triage](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/code-review/risk-triage.md) | A whole-PR risk assessment shaped by organization and repository policy. |

See [How Gitar Works](https://docs.gitar.ai/how-gitar-works.md) for the context used during review, including web documentation and connected knowledge sources.

## Large PRs and review volume

Gitar supports unlimited changed files per PR. Large changes remain eligible for review, including changes spread across a monorepo.

Gitar prioritizes relevant code and condenses repetitive changes to keep large diffs reviewable. Generated files and other low-value content may be excluded from review.

Enterprise includes [unlimited review volume per author](https://docs.gitar.ai/account-billing/plans.md#enterprise-scale), including allowed bot authors. Other plans follow the [usage policy](https://docs.gitar.ai/account-billing/plans.md#usage-limits).

## How It Works

Code reviews run automatically when:

* A new pull request is created
* New commits are pushed to an open PR

Gitar skips a PR containing only a single revert commit. This also applies when the original change was never reviewed by Gitar.

Push any commit beyond the revert and Gitar reviews the pull request as usual, because at that point it is no longer a plain revert. Everything else still runs either way, including CI analysis and rule evaluation.

## Review depth

Review depth controls which verified findings Gitar reports.

| Setting | What to expect |
| - | - |
| Focused | Prioritizes higher-impact findings. |
| Thorough | Includes smaller verified issues, with more comments to assess. |

Enterprise organization admins choose the default under **Settings -> Configuration -> Review depth**. To set a different depth for a repository, select **Customize** on its row and choose **Focused** or **Thorough**. Changes take effect on the next review, including existing PRs.

Repositories inherit the organization default until an override is saved. Resetting an override restores inheritance. Previously saved review depth settings are retained.

## Custom Code Review Instructions

Add your own rules, checks, or gotchas to tailor the review to your project. Commit a markdown file under the **`.gitar/review`** directory. Use several files to organize instructions by topic.

Gitar's own repository, for example, has a `gitar-gotchas.md` covering conventions specific to that codebase. One of them is to use `info!` for logging that needs operational visibility and leave `debug!` for local debugging, since its telemetry only renders logs at severity `info` or higher.

One file can pull in another with the `@` syntax, so shared guidance lives in one place. See [Custom Review Instructions](https://docs.gitar.ai/configuration/repository-config.md#custom-review-instructions) for the directory layout and include resolution.

## Review Output

Gitar publishes review feedback in two places on your PR:

* **Inline review comments**: every unresolved finding is posted on the exact file and line it applies to, so feedback lands where you're reading the code.
* **Dashboard comment, Code Review section**: a consolidated view on the Gitar dashboard comment showing the overall verdict, severity breakdown, and resolved-finding tracking.

The dashboard comment is the single source of truth for the overall state of a PR, holding the code review summary, CI analysis, and rule evaluations in one place. When you push new commits, Gitar updates that comment instead of posting a new one, so your PR timeline stays clean.

Resolved findings move into a collapsible section as you push fixes, so what is left to address stays at the top.

The **Cross-Repo** and **Cross-PR** categories only appear when [Cross-Repo Analysis](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/cross-repo-analysis.md) or [Cross-PR Analysis](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/cross-pr-analysis.md) is turned on for your organization.

To change how that summary reads, set [review summary instructions](https://docs.gitar.ai/configuration/settings.md#review-summary-instructions) for your organization.

Code Review in Dashboard Comment

Each finding includes:

* **Category**: Security, Bug, Performance, Edge Case, Code Quality, Cross-Repo, or Cross-PR
* **Severity**: Critical, Important, or Minor
* **Short description**: One-line summary of the issue
* **Details**: Expanded explanation with a link to the specific file and line
* **Citations**: links to available sources for learned guidance. See [Citations in findings](#citations-in-findings).

### Citations in findings

Citations make team-specific review advice traceable. When a finding relies on learned guidance, its explanation can link to the instruction or earlier conversation behind that guidance.

The link appears within the finding, alongside the reasoning about the changed code. See [Knowledge source citations](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/knowledge.md#source-citations) for how sources are retained and when a citation becomes a link.

### Verification

**Verification** follows Code Review and collects recorded outcomes, including linked issue objectives and rule results. It can appear without a code review. Covered objectives and checked expectations describe assessments against code, without claiming that runtime tests ran.

The header keeps one compact badge per feature, such as `Objectives 5/7`, `Rules 3/4 met` and `Repos 1 inspected`. Knowledge shows check and lens counts. The rule ratio excludes skipped checks and recorded actions.

The section opens for unmet requirements. A knowledge-backed finding opens it while that finding remains open in the current review. Settled outcomes collapse, even when Code Review still requests changes.

| Row | What it reports |
| - | - |
| Functional validation | Active objective counts, linked issues and objective names. |
| Rules | Check outcomes and recorded actions, with successful names visible in normal mode. |
| Auto-approval | Approved, Withheld or Not evaluated. |
| Knowledge | Expectations explicitly met and retained finding citations, with finding links. |
| Cross-repo | Recorded inspections and open impacts, or selected repositories when inspection status is unknown. |

Each feature has its own collapsed section and outcome badges. Open a feature to read up to five successful names. Unmet requirements stay visible without another toggle. `gitar display:verbose` adds remaining names and supporting evidence. Platforms without collapsible HTML show the same results as headings and compact rows.

Code Review still requests changes while Verification shows four covered objectives after opening its feature section

The [risk label](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/code-review/risk-triage.md#where-risk-appears) appears separately in expanded Code Review, since risk describes the whole change rather than which checks ran.

## Providing Feedback

Feedback controls how Gitar handles findings on the current PR:

* Reply to a finding with an explanation. A confirmed fix resolves it. An invalid finding is dismissed. A decision to leave it unfixed closes it without counting it as fixed. On GitLab, replies to inline findings need no `gitar` prefix.
* **Reply `gitar fix`**: Every inline finding includes a "Reply `gitar fix` to apply this suggestion" footer. One reply and Gitar pushes the fix.
* **One-click apply**: On GitHub, check the box next to a suggested fix to apply it. On GitLab, react with the checkmark emoji. Gitar commits the fix to your branch. When a finding has multiple fixes, each one is numbered.
* Resolving a finding thread on GitHub closes it without marking it fixed or invalid. Unresolving that thread reopens it. On GitLab, a thumbs-down reaction dismisses a finding.
* **Stale findings**: When code is deleted or rewritten between review iterations, Gitar automatically resolves findings that pointed at the removed code.
* **Ambiguous replies**: If your reply is unclear, Gitar asks a follow-up question instead of guessing.

Acknowledging a finding or promising a follow-up keeps it open. Acknowledged findings still count toward merge blocking and do not count as fixed. The [Reviews dashboard](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/insights.md#reviews) shows their recorded reasons and source replies when available.

If an accepted fix fails, the inline comment shows **Fix could not be applied**. The failed attempt does not automatically start another one. Request another fix in a reply or push a correction.

Your feedback persists across review iterations. Gitar won't re-report issues you've already dismissed.

With [Knowledge](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/knowledge.md) enabled, explanations in review comments can also teach Gitar conventions for future PRs.

## Merge Blocking

Gitar can block PR merges based on its code review verdict severity. Configure a threshold in your [organization settings](https://docs.gitar.ai/configuration/settings.md), and Gitar submits a blocking review on the PR when the verdict meets or exceeds it. See [Block Merge](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/code-review/block-merge.md) for details.

## Auto-Approve

Gitar can automatically approve PRs after a clean review based on criteria you define. See [Auto-Approve](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/code-review/auto-approve.md) for details.

## Auto-Merge

After auto-approve, Gitar can arm your platform's native auto-merge so the PR merges once all other checks pass. See [Auto-Merge](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/code-review/auto-merge.md) for details.

# AI Code Review That Fixes Your Code

> AI code review that automatically fixes broken builds, failing tests, and code review feedback. Ship cleaner code faster.

# AI Code Review That Fixes Your Code

Gitar goes past comments and fixes broken builds, failing tests, and code review feedback. Ship cleaner code faster.

### [Code Review](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/code-review.md)

AI-powered code review that catches security issues, bugs, and code quality problems before merge.

### [CI Failure Analysis](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/ci-failure-analysis.md)

Automatically detect failing builds and tests, analyze root cause, and push fixes to your PR.

### [Repository Rules](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/rules.md)

Create automated workflows using natural language rules. No code required.

## Start Here

> [card] [Start using Gitar](https://docs.gitar.ai/quickstart.md)
>
> Install Gitar and see it work on a PR in under 5 minutes. Free 14-day trial, no credit card required.

> [card] [Connect your code](https://docs.gitar.ai/connecting-code/platform-support.md)
>
> GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps. See the supported hosting options.

> [card] [Set up SSO](https://docs.gitar.ai/administration/sso.md)
>
> SAML single sign-on with Okta or any SAML 2.0 provider

## See It In Action

Here's what happens when Gitar reviews a PR with a failing test:

> [tab] Before Gitar
>
> ```text theme={null}
> CI Failed: test_user_authentication
>
> AssertionError: expected 200 but got 401
>   at test_user_authentication (tests/auth.test.js:42)
> ```
>
> You read the log, find the missing auth header in the test setup, push a fix, and wait for CI again.

> [tab] With Gitar
>
> ```text theme={null}
> CI Failed: test_user_authentication
>
> Gitar analyzed the failure:
> "Test is missing auth header in request setup.
>  Adding Bearer token to test fixture."
>
> Gitar pushed fix -> CI passing
> ```
>
> You read the fix commit and merge.

## What Makes Gitar Different

> [card] Fixes, Not Comments
>
> Traditional code review tools stop at a comment. Gitar pushes the fix to your PR.

> [card] [CI-Aware](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/ci-failure-analysis.md#recovery-after-a-gitar-fix)
>
> When a Gitar fix causes CI to fail, automatic recovery can attempt a follow-up fix. See the recovery conditions in CI Failure Analysis.

> [card] Works Where You Work
>
> Review comments and fix requests stay in the PR. Organization settings and insights are available in the Gitar dashboard.

> [card] Zero Config
>
> Install the app and Gitar starts working immediately. Customize later with `.gitar/` rules.

# Repository Customization

> Configure Gitar's behavior at the repository level with instruction files, review rules, and the .gitar directory

Gitar reads its per-repository configuration out of your codebase: AI instruction files, custom review instructions, and automation rules. All of it is version-controlled alongside the code it applies to.

## AI Instruction Files

Gitar recognizes the following files as AI instruction sources:

| File | Description |
| - | - |
| `AGENTS.md` | General AI agent instructions for your repository. `agent.md` and `agents.md` are read too |
| `CLAUDE.md` | Claude-specific instructions and conventions |
| `.cursorrules` | Cursor-compatible instruction file |
| `.cursor/rules/*` | Directory of Cursor rule files |
| `.claude/rules/*` | Directory of rule files kept alongside `.claude/skills` |

Both rule directories are read one level deep, so a rule at `.claude/rules/backend/api.md` is not picked up. Keep rule files directly in the directory.

When Gitar processes a PR, it reads these files to understand your repository's conventions, coding standards, and best practices. This context is used during both code review and CI failure fixing.

> [!NOTE]
>
> These files are read automatically, with no additional configuration needed. Gitar loads them from your repository root on every PR. When the agent works inside a subdirectory during a run, it also picks up instruction files and rule directories between that subdirectory and the root.

### Including other files

If your conventions already live in another file, such as `guidelines.md`, reference it from any of the files above with `@` followed by its path. Gitar replaces the reference with that file's content.

```markdown AGENTS.md theme={null}
Follow the commit and naming conventions below.

@guidelines.md
@docs/architecture.md
```

Paths resolve from the folder of the file that contains them, then from the repository root, and must stay inside the repository. Put each reference on its own line or follow it with a space, since trailing punctuation becomes part of the path. References inside code blocks or inline code are ignored. Included files can reference other files as well.

You can also place the file in `.gitar/instructions/`, where every Markdown file loads for all Gitar agents.

## The .gitar Directory

The `.gitar` directory is the primary location for Gitar-specific configuration:

```text theme={null}
your-repo/
  .gitar/
    rules/        # Repository rules (automation workflows)
      *.md
    review/       # Custom code review instructions
      *.md
    skills/       # Reusable procedures the agent can run on request
      <name>/SKILL.md
    instructions/ # Instructions every Gitar agent reads, not just review
      *.md
    cross-repo.md # Guidance for Cross-Repo Analysis
    config/       # Per-repository criteria files
      apply.md
      approve.md
      merge.md
      risk.md
```

| Directory | Purpose |
| - | - |
| `.gitar/rules/` | Natural-language automation rules that trigger actions when conditions are met |
| `.gitar/review/` | Custom instructions that tailor what Gitar looks for during code review |
| `.gitar/skills/` | Named procedures loaded on demand. See [Skills](https://docs.gitar.ai/integrations/skills.md) |
| `.gitar/instructions/` | Instructions loaded into every Gitar agent, not only code review |
| `.gitar/cross-repo.md` | Guidance for cross-repository checks. See [Cross-Repo Analysis](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/cross-repo-analysis.md) |
| `.gitar/config/apply.md` | This repository's auto-apply criteria. See [Auto-Apply](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/code-review/auto-apply.md) |
| `.gitar/config/approve.md` | This repository's auto-approve criteria. See [Auto-Approve](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/code-review/auto-approve.md) |
| `.gitar/config/merge.md` | This repository's auto-merge criteria. See [Auto-Merge](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/code-review/auto-merge.md) |
| `.gitar/config/risk.md` | Repository risk guidance that can raise the organization's assessment. See [Risk Triage](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/code-review/risk-triage.md) |

`.claude/skills/`, `.agents/skills/`, and `.github/skills/` are read as well, so skills already kept for Claude Code, Codex, or Copilot need no second copy.

AI instruction files, skills, `.gitar/rules/`, `.gitar/review/`, `.gitar/instructions/` and `.gitar/cross-repo.md` can live in [configuration repositories](https://docs.gitar.ai/configuration/configuration-repository.md) instead of being committed to each repository.

Select up to three configuration repositories to share configuration across the organization. Shared `approve.md`, `merge.md`, and `risk.md` files extend the organization baseline. Each repository's own files apply on top. `apply.md` stays per repository.

Gitar reads `apply.md`, `approve.md`, and `merge.md` from the default branch. Edits to those files take effect after they merge. Risk guidance also considers additions in the PR, as described in [Risk Triage](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/code-review/risk-triage.md#add-repository-guidance).

## Custom Review Instructions

The `.gitar/review/` directory lets you tailor Gitar's code review to your project's specific requirements. Add one or more markdown files containing instructions, checks, or gotchas that Gitar should consider during reviews.

Multiple files can organize instructions by topic, for example separate files for security rules, performance guidelines, and project-specific gotchas.

**Example:** A file named `.gitar/review/gotchas.md` that documents codebase-specific patterns:

```markdown theme={null}
# Logging Gotchas

- Use `info!` for logging that requires operational visibility
- Leave `debug!` for local debugging only
- Our telemetry only renders logs with severity `info` or higher
```

### Including Specific Files

You can include content from other files using the `@` syntax with a relative path. Paths are first resolved relative to the source file, with a fallback to the repository root if not found.

**Example:** Given the following directory structure:

```text theme={null}
your-repo/
  .gitar/
    rust_best_practices.md
    review/
      gotchas.md
  shared/
    common_rules.md
```

From `.gitar/review/gotchas.md`, you can include files using either approach:

```markdown theme={null}
# Gotchas for Rust Code

@../rust_best_practices.md

@shared/common_rules.md

# Other project-specific gotchas
...
```

* `@../rust_best_practices.md` - resolved relative to `gotchas.md`, one level up from `review/`
* `@shared/common_rules.md` - not found relative to `review/`, so falls back to repo root resolution

This works recursively, so an included file can itself include other files.

## Repository Rules

Repository rules let you create automated workflows using natural language, specified in `.gitar/rules/*.md` files. When conditions defined in the rule are met on a PR, Gitar automatically executes the specified actions.

See the [Repository Rules documentation](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/rules.md) for full details, syntax, and examples.

## Organization-Level Settings

Organization-level settings set the defaults every connected repository starts from. See [Settings](https://docs.gitar.ai/configuration/settings.md) for what they cover.

# Auto-Approve

> Automatically approve pull requests after a clean code review

## Overview

Auto-approve lets Gitar submit an approving review on your behalf after a clean code review. You define criteria in natural language, and if they are met, Gitar approves the PR without any manual action required.

> [card] Criteria-Driven
>
> Define approval conditions in natural language, or use the default behavior with no criteria at all

> [card] Post-Review Only
>
> Only runs after a clean code review with no blocking findings

> [card] Per-Repo Control
>
> Extend org criteria per repository with a config file

## How It Works

**1. Code review completes**

Gitar reviews the PR as usual. Important or critical findings withhold approval. Approval is also withheld when the configured merge blocking threshold includes unresolved suggestions.

**2. Criteria are checked**

Gitar evaluates your configured criteria against the whole PR, including its changed files and unresolved findings. If no criteria are configured, Gitar approves the PR when the review found no blocking issues.

**3. Approval is submitted**

Gitar submits an approval on the connected code host. The dashboard comment shows the approval and the rationale.

## Enabling Auto-Approve

Auto-approve is configured in your organization settings:

1. Navigate to **Settings -> Configuration** in the Gitar dashboard
2. Open the **Behavior** section
3. Enable the **Auto-approve PRs based on code review** toggle
4. Optionally, enter custom approval criteria in the text area that appears

Criteria are written in natural language. Examples:

* "Only approve if the changes are limited to documentation or test files"
* "Approve changes to the `docs/` directory or files ending in `.md`"
* "Skip approval if the PR modifies authentication or payment logic"

> [!NOTE]
>
> Auto-approval criteria are evaluated against the PR metadata, changed files, and code review
> results, not CI pipeline status. Gitar does not verify conditions like "tests pass" or "linting
> is green". Enforce those with your platform's branch protection or merge checks.
>
> Criteria also cannot call integration tools. Naming a Jira, Slack, or [custom MCP](https://docs.gitar.ai/integrations/custom-integrations.md)
> tool in your criteria does not make its result an approval condition, and results from earlier
> integration calls are not passed into the evaluation.

### Use PR risk in criteria

Approval criteria can use Gitar's whole-PR risk assessment, for example, "Approve only low- or medium-risk changes." [Risk Triage](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/code-review/risk-triage.md) explains the levels and team-defined policy.

Risk restricts approval after review. Low risk does not bypass blocking findings, and an unavailable assessment does not meet a risk-dependent condition unless the criteria explicitly allow it.

### Require code owner or human approval

On GitHub, criteria can use `CODEOWNERS` and human reviews. For example:

```text theme={null}
Only approve when a code owner other than the author has approved the current head.
```

Gitar reads `CODEOWNERS` from the PR's target branch. It checks who owns the changed files and whether each review applies to the current commit. Team ownership requires the GitHub App's organization **Members: read** permission.

If ownership or review evidence cannot be read, the condition is unmet and Gitar withholds approval. These criteria are unavailable on other code hosts, where they also withhold approval.

### Default Behavior (No Criteria)

With the toggle enabled and no criteria in organization settings, configuration repositories, or `.gitar/config/approve.md`, Gitar approves PRs with no blocking findings. Minor suggestions may remain unless the configured merge blocking threshold includes them.

## After Approval

When auto-approve fires, you can optionally chain additional actions from the same settings section.

### `gitar-approved` Label

Enable **Apply gitar-approved label** to mark approved PRs. See [`gitar-approved`](https://docs.gitar.ai/labels#gitar-approved) for label behavior.

### Auto-Merge

Enable **Auto-merge PRs** to merge automatically after approval. See [Auto-Merge](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/code-review/auto-merge.md) for platform prerequisites and merge methods.

## Per-Repo Criteria

You can define criteria at the repository level by placing a Markdown file at `.gitar/config/approve.md`. Repo criteria work on their own or alongside org-level criteria.

Gitar reads this file from the default branch. Changes take effect after they merge, so a PR cannot change its own approval policy. If Gitar cannot verify the file, it withholds approval for that run.

See [Repository Customization](https://docs.gitar.ai/configuration/repository-config.md) for more on the `.gitar` directory and how repo-level config files work.

```bash theme={null}
mkdir -p .gitar/config
echo "Only approve if no database migrations are included." > .gitar/config/approve.md
```

### Combination Logic

Organization criteria include shared approval policy from selected [configuration repositories](https://docs.gitar.ai/configuration/configuration-repository.md).

| Org criteria | Repo file | What happens |
| - | - | - |
| Set | Present | Both are combined, so the PR must satisfy all criteria |
| Set | Absent | Org criteria only |
| Empty | Present | Repo file criteria only |
| Empty | Absent | Default: approve unless the review has blocking findings |

## Platform Behavior

Auto-approve works on GitHub, GitLab, Azure DevOps, and both Bitbucket editions. See [Platform Support](https://docs.gitar.ai/connecting-code/platform-support.md) for preview availability.

> [accordion] GitHub
>
> Gitar submits an approving review on the PR. If your branch protection rules require an approving review, this satisfies that requirement.
>
> The review body reads: *"Gitar has auto-approved this PR"* with a link to your auto-approve settings.
>
> If auto-merge is also enabled, the review body mentions that auto-merge has been armed.

> [accordion] GitLab
>
> Gitar approves the MR via the API. If your approval rules list Gitar as an eligible approver, this counts toward the required approval count.
>
> If auto-merge is also enabled, Gitar calls the GitLab API to arm auto-merge after approval.

> [accordion] Azure DevOps
>
> Gitar sets an Approved vote on the PR using the connected service account. If auto-merge is enabled, Gitar also enables auto-complete.

> [accordion] Bitbucket
>
> Gitar approves the PR on Cloud and Data Center. Bitbucket Cloud has no auto-merge to arm. On Data Center, Gitar merges the PR itself once Bitbucket's merge checks pass.

## Revocation

Each new review checks the current PR against the current criteria. On GitHub, resolving finding threads can trigger another approval evaluation without a push once the review is eligible. The dashboard shows **Re-evaluating** while that check runs.

If a new push introduces blocking findings, Gitar revokes its previous approval:

* On GitHub, Gitar dismisses its approving review.
* On GitLab, Gitar calls the unapprove API.
* On Azure DevOps, Gitar clears its approval vote.
* On Bitbucket, Gitar removes its approval.
* If auto-merge was armed, it is also disabled.

If the `gitar-approved` label was applied, Gitar removes it when the approval is revoked.

> [!NOTE]
>
> If Gitar cannot complete approval evaluation, it skips approval for that run.

# Functional Validation

> Check whether a PR implements what its linked issue asked for

## Overview

Functional validation reads the issues a PR claims to close, breaks each one into individual objectives, and judges every objective against the diff. The result is a **Functional validation** row under Verification in the [Gitar dashboard comment](https://docs.gitar.ai/gitar-dashboard.md), one block per linked issue, least complete first.

> [card] Objective by Objective
>
> Each requirement in the issue is tracked on its own, so a PR that does most of the work reads as partial rather than done

> [card] Re-Judged on Every Push
>
> New commits are re-checked against the same objectives, so the section keeps up with the branch

> [!NOTE]
>
> Functional validation is included on the **Enterprise** plan. A tracker issue needs that integration connected. Your code host's own issues need nothing connected.

## Supported Issue Sources

| Issue source | Referenced as | Needs |
| - | - | - |
| [Jira](https://docs.gitar.ai/integrations/jira.md) | `PROJ-123` | Jira integration connected |
| [Linear](https://docs.gitar.ai/integrations/linear.md) | `ENG-45` | Linear integration connected |
| [Plane](https://docs.gitar.ai/integrations/plane.md) | `ENG-45` | Plane integration connected |
| [YouTrack](https://docs.gitar.ai/integrations/youtrack.md) | `SP-7` | YouTrack integration connected |
| GitHub issues | `#123` | nothing |
| GitLab issues | `#123` | nothing |
| Azure DevOps work items | linked to the PR, or `AB#123` | nothing |
| Bitbucket Cloud issues | `#123` | the repo's issue tracker enabled |

Bitbucket Data Center has no issue tracker of its own, so link a Jira issue there instead.

A tracker key is the same shape on Jira, Linear, Plane, and YouTrack, so connect one tracker per organization. With more than one connected, Gitar reads the key against Jira first, then Linear, then Plane, then YouTrack.

## How It Works

**1. Gitar finds the linked issue**

Gitar looks for issue keys in the PR title, description, and branch name. Nothing is linked unless the PR claims the issue, so a passing mention is ignored.

**2. The issue becomes a list of objectives**

Gitar reads the issue text from its source and derives the concrete objectives it asks for.

**3. Each objective is judged against the diff**

Every objective is marked covered or not covered based on the current diff. Pushing new commits re-runs the judgement, and editing the issue reconciles the objective list against it.

**4. Objectives appear in Verification**

The section is added to the existing Gitar comment on the PR. Gitar posts no separate comment and adds no status check.

## Linking an Issue

Reference the issue in the PR title, the PR description, or the branch name, the way you already do to close an issue. A tracker key (`PROJ-123`) and your code host's own issue number (`#123`) both work.

A `#123` refers to an issue in the PR's own repository. Another repository's issue (`other/repo#123`) is not linked.

On Azure DevOps, work items attached to the PR are picked up directly, so there is nothing to write in the description.

For Jira, Gitar also reads accessible parent issues to clarify the linked issue's requirements. Parent objectives do not become additional objectives for the PR.

On public repositories, validation uses only issues from the same repository. External tracker content is excluded.

With validation enabled, Gitar links issues it can read and checks the PR against their objectives. Organization admins can turn **Validate PRs against linked issues** on or off under **Settings -> Configuration -> Behavior**. Uncovered objectives are reported in the comment and do not block merging.

## Reading the Section

The Functional validation row counts active objectives across linked issues, for example **3 covered / 5 objectives**. Each issue keeps its link and count, with the least-covered issue first. Dropped objectives stay excluded.

A partly covered issue is scope information, since an earlier PR may have delivered the rest. Uncovered objectives appear under **Other objectives on this issue, possibly covered elsewhere**. They do not block merging.

Verification opens while any objective is uncovered. Once all recorded outcomes are settled, it collapses. Opening Functional validation reveals up to five objective names across the linked issues. `gitar display:verbose` adds the remaining names and summaries.

Verification showing covered objectives and other scope from a linked issue

On platforms without collapsible HTML, the same content appears as headings and lists. A linked issue with no active objectives contributes no validation body, while other Verification outcomes can still appear.

[Risk Triage](https://docs.gitar.ai/features/code-review/risk-triage.md) separately assesses the impact of the whole change. Objective coverage does not imply Code Review approval or executed runtime tests.

## Changing the Issue

Objectives track the issue rather than a snapshot of it. Add a requirement and it shows up as not covered on the next run. Remove one and it stops counting against the PR: the objective total drops instead of the completion count going up, so cutting scope can never read as work finished.

## Limits

A PR validates at most 5 linked issues. Extra keys beyond that are ignored.

Gitar reads the issue text but never writes to it. Objectives, statuses, and counts live only in the PR comment - your tracker stays the source of truth. To have Gitar post back to the issue on merge, see [Jira](https://docs.gitar.ai/integrations/jira.md), [Linear](https://docs.gitar.ai/integrations/linear.md), [Plane](https://docs.gitar.ai/integrations/plane.md), and [YouTrack](https://docs.gitar.ai/integrations/youtrack.md).

Objectives belong to the PR being reviewed. Two PRs against the same issue each track their own set, and Gitar has no combined per-issue view.

## Related

> [card] [Jira Integration](https://docs.gitar.ai/integrations/jira.md)
>
> Connect Jira so Gitar can read linked issues

> [card] [Linear Integration](https://docs.gitar.ai/integrations/linear.md)
>
> Connect Linear so Gitar can read linked issues

> [card] [Plane Integration](https://docs.gitar.ai/integrations/plane.md)
>
> Connect a Plane workspace so Gitar can read linked work items

> [card] [The Gitar Dashboard](https://docs.gitar.ai/gitar-dashboard.md)
>
> Where Verification is rendered

>
